name: sliceslice (Rust AVX2 substring search)
baseline: Rust std String::find (also memmem, twoway crates and WojciechMula/sse4-strstr in the same table); not libc
workload: Criterion 'i386' benchmark (benches/i386.rs at tag v0.2.1; now bench/benches/i386.rs): short haystack: words of data/words.txt sorted by length, each searched in every later word; long haystack: every word searched in data/i386.txt (read with fs::read and from_utf8_lossy at v0.2.1, include_bytes in the current bench); single-pattern substring search returning a bool. sliceslice and memmem searchers are constructed outside the timed loop; String::find, twoway and sse4-strstr build per call.
claimed_speedup: README table (criterion time, lower is better): short haystack String::find 335.56 ms vs sliceslice DynamicAvx2Searcher 79.416 ms (about 4.2x faster, derived from page data); long haystack 345.01 ms vs 35.181 ms (about 9.8x faster, derived from page data). sse4-strstr avx2_strstr_v2 measures 75.515 ms and 38.579 ms in the same table.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.46.0 and gcc 9.3.0 (README). The published table was produced by the v0.2.1-era harness (benches/i386.rs at tag v0.2.1, criterion 0.3, no [profile.bench] override, so cargo bench defaults at opt-level 3; the sse4-strstr C++ wrapper is compiled by sse4-strstr/build.rs with -std=c++11 -march=native). The current bench/ crate (criterion 0.5, [profile.bench] lto = true, codegen-units = 1) came later and was not used for the README numbers.
hardware: HP EliteDesk 800 G2 Tower PC, Intel Core i7-6700 @ 3.40GHz, 16GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04.1 LTS
tradeoffs: Rust crate (no C API); x86 AVX2 searcher built on Wojciech Mula's SIMD-friendly algorithm with the needle fixed at construction, and unlike sse4-strstr it never reads past the end of the haystack (README footnote).
caveats: Baseline is Rust 1.46 std String::find (2020), not libc memmem or any C++ std; README numbers are for sliceslice 0.2.0 on 2020 toolchains with the v0.2.1 harness, and the README table omits the memchr::memmem rows the current bench now runs. The benchmark is asymmetric: sliceslice (and memmem) searchers are prebuilt outside the timed loop while String::find rebuilds its Two-Way searcher per call, so needle preprocessing is excluded only for the prebuilt rows. In BurntSushi's memchr rebar record (benchmarks/record/x86_64/2026-07-30.csv, sliceslice 0.4.3) sliceslice oneshot is about 2.17x faster than libc memmem by geomean of medians over 39 benchmarks (faster on 30) and about 3.9x faster than Rust std memmem oneshot (faster on 34 of 38), but prebuilt sliceslice beats memchr 2.8.3 prebuilt on only 15 of 42 benchmarks (geomean 0.90x) (derived from that CSV; older records 2023-12-29 and 2025-09-25 give 2.08x and 2.14x vs libc). Open issue #97 (January 2025, no maintainer reply) reports that Avx2Searcher can read past the end of the haystack (OOB read in vector_search_in_chunk); the API is unsafe and x86 AVX2 only; issue #47 recorded a performance regression with Rust 1.52.
found_via: WebSearch 'SIMD-friendly substring search strstr memmem AVX2 SSE4.2 speedup over glibc github' surfaced cloudflare/sliceslice-rs; opened README.md, bench/Cargo.toml, bench/benches/i386.rs

name: WojciechMula/toys avx512-string (AVX512F strlen, strchr, strrchr, strcmp)
baseline: libc strlen/strchr/strrchr/strcmp via <cstring> (labelled 'std' in the harness; libc version not stated)
workload: strlen/strchr/strrchr/strcmp over 10 kB strings on a Knights Landing CPU, AVX512F kernels (SWAR tricks since AVX512F has no byte ops) versus the stdlib routine.
tradeoffs: Requires AVX512F (Xeon Phi KNL, Skylake-X and later). The strlen kernel uses unaligned 64-byte loads that can read past the terminator and across a page boundary, so it is only safe on padded buffers (the harness pads by 64 bytes). Only four functions (strlen, strchr, strrchr, strcmp); no memcpy/memchr.
caveats: Author says the tests 'aren't very good' and do not cover a range of string lengths: one 10 KiB buffer filled with '?', the terminator (or target char) moved through every position, 5 iterations, gettimeofday timing, no repetitions or variance. Measured once in October 2016 on one old CPU with GCC 5.4.3 (not an official GCC release number; 5.4.0 and 5.5.0 exist); the glibc version and which of its ifunc variants ran on KNL are not stated, so the baseline may be a weak SSE2 path (the 16x strrchr gain points that way). The AVX512F kernels use unaligned 64-byte loads with no page-boundary handling (avx512f_strlen does _mm512_loadu_si512(s + len) in a loop), so they can read up to 63 bytes past the terminator and fault at the end of a mapped page; the benchmark pads every buffer by 64 bytes, so they are not drop-in libc replacements without aligned or masked loads. speed_strlen discards the strlen result (the other three harnesses accumulate into a volatile counter); the measured times look like real work. avx512f-strcmp.cpp was simplified by KWillets on 2020-04-06 (commit 8759381, removes a redundant zero2 mask, not a correctness fix), after the README numbers were taken. The README lists custom scalar versions too but reports only std vs AVX512F. Date shown is the last commit touching avx512-string; the toys repo itself was last pushed 2026-04-08. An SSE2 version of the same four functions lives in WojciechMula/sse2string, whose README gives no numbers.

name: jnettlet/cortex_a72_memcpy (Cortex-A72 tuned AArch64 memcpy/memset)
baseline: glibc memcpy (the 'memcpy' row) and Arm Optimized Routines memcpy (__memcpy_aarch64, __memcpy_aarch64_simd)
workload: Arm optimized-routines memcpy benchmark (string/bench/memcpy.c) on a Cortex-A72: random copies (16384 copies with lengths from a SPEC2017-derived size distribution under 4 KB) over 32K to 1024K working sets, aligned and unaligned medium copies 8 B to 512 B, large copies 1K to 64K, and forwards/backwards unaligned memmove 1K to 64K, in bytes per ns.
claimed_speedup: README: 'We are now pretty equivalent or faster than glibc's memcpy and Arm's optimized library memcpy on the optimized library's memcpy benchmark.' Aligned medium memcpy (bytes/ns): 16 B __memcpy_a72 4.40 vs memcpy 2.51; 32 B 8.79 vs 5.03; 64 B 12.80 vs 9.38 (about 1.75x, 1.75x, 1.36x, derived from page data). Random memcpy average 2.01 vs 1.97; large copies equal within 1-2%; unaligned backwards memmove 64K 11.69 vs 6.54.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark. The library's Makefile builds the assembly with CPPFLAGS -fPIC -g -fno-inline -fno-builtin-inline -fno-inline-functions -fno-builtin and LDFLAGS -shared; compiler version unstated.
hardware: Cortex-A72 (board, SoC and clock not stated)
tradeoffs: AArch64 Cortex-A72 only; built as libmemcpy.so for LD_PRELOAD or /etc/ld.so.preload; the stated purpose is fixing copies to memory-mapped device memory (framebuffers, SPDK) by reordering two stores in the 96-byte path, not general speed.
caveats: The repo's stated purpose is a device-memory fix (re-ordered stores in the 96-byte path for framebuffers/SPDK); the code is an initial import of Arm optimized-routines memcpy (Arm MIT header; memset.S is MIT OR Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception; COPYING is MIT, Solidrun Ltd 2021), loaded via LD_PRELOAD. README tables (added July 2022) give no compiler, flags, board, SoC or clock, and the code was reworked again in January 2024 after the numbers were published. The 'memcpy' row is the system libc (presumably glibc). Gains are mostly small aligned sizes (8-64 B: 1.36-1.75x over libc, 1.18-1.50x over __memcpy_aarch64); random and large copies are within 1-2%; the backwards-memmove 64K win (11.69 vs 6.54) is shared by Arm's __memcpy_aarch64 (11.67); unaligned 64 B (8.46 vs 9.35) and backwards memmove 1K-8K (e.g. 16.48 vs 16.70 at 4K) are slightly slower than libc.

name: KmStrSearch (Windows kernel UTF-8 and UTF-16 substring search)
baseline: Windows kernel CRT strstr and wcsstr (MSVC runtime; not glibc or musl)
workload: Kernel driver harness (Shared/KmStrSearchShared.h): one worker thread per engine runs Find or CRT strstr/wcsstr in a loop for about 2 s, GB/s = whole-buffer bytes per call times calls over elapsed time (GB = 2^30 bytes). Three inputs at 40 B / 256 B / 10 KB / 1 MB (8-bit, double for 16-bit): 'Needle In The Haystack' placed near the end of a buffer of all 'A' (no text character occurs in the pattern, the best case for Boyer-Moore-Horspool skipping); 'aaaaaaaaab' near the end of all-'a' text; and a repeated log line with a 33-character pattern near the end. Hybrid BMH with SWAR, AVX2 and AVX-512BW engines and a size-based 'Smart Auto' router versus the kernel CRT.
claimed_speedup: i7-1165G7, 8-bit, GB/s (CRT baseline vs Smart Auto): 10 KB 22.38 vs 45.71, 1 MB 22.66 vs 85.93; 16-bit 20 KB 26.67 vs 68.43. Worse on small buffers: 40 B 3.61 vs 1.95, 256 B 15.03 vs 4.88. README: on mismatched dense text CRT collapses to 0.21-0.37 GB/s while the hybrid delivers 49-81 GB/s, 'up to 385x faster'.
tradeoffs: Windows kernel-mode (WDK driver) code: routes small buffers to a SWAR path to avoid the KeSaveExtendedProcessorState cost of entering vector mode, and uses AVX2/AVX-512BW or ARM64 NEON for larger buffers. Uses 8 KB (UTF-16) skip tables allocated from paged pool. Not a user-mode library; the README says user-mode (TestUm) timings cannot be trusted.
caveats: Very new, single-author exploration with 0 stars and 4 commits ('not strictly benchmark-driven during its design'); no repetition counts or variance; MSVC version and build configuration unstated. The README calls the harness multi-threaded and memory-bus saturating, but RunPerformanceSuiteT calls StartThreads(pMgr, 1, ...), so each figure is single-thread throughput. Throughput counts the whole buffer per call even though BMH skips most bytes, so the 80-105 GB/s figures at 1 MB are not memory bandwidth; the 'standard' input is the best case for BMH (text all 'A', pattern contains no 'A'). The 'up to 385x' dense-text figure comes from a pattern whose last character never occurs in the text, so the hybrid reduces to a vectorized memchr while the CRT's naive strstr does O(N*M) work; glibc's two-way strstr would not collapse this way. The baseline is the Windows kernel CRT strstr/wcsstr, not glibc or musl; on the VMware guest it measures only 1.35-1.67 GB/s on 256 B to 1 MB inputs (about 15x below the same CRT on bare metal). Loses to CRT on tiny and small buffers on bare metal (40 B 3.61 vs 1.95 GB/s, 256 B 15.03 vs 4.88 GB/s for 8-bit Smart Auto). User-mode build is declared untrustworthy for timing. Kernel driver telemetry only; no independent reproduction.

name: nadavrot/memset_benchmark (AVX2 assembly memset and memcpy)
language: Assembly (x86-64 AVX2, AT&T .S) with C/C++ harness
baseline: glibc memset and memcpy (with and without PLT indirection, 'libc@plt' and 'libc'), also musl and folly (memcpy chart)
workload: README charts: (1) random-size batches, 10M calls x 20 samples (median), size and destination offset each drawn from a pre-computed random u8 sequence (0 to 255 bytes), nop-function call overhead subtracted; memset compares libc@plt, libc and asm_memset, memcpy compares libc@plt, libc, folly and asm_memcpy. workload: test64 times libc strstr, std::string::find and the 64-bit SWAR first/last-byte filter (10 iterations each, gettimeofday) for every unique word extracted from i386.txt by make_words.sh, so each search succeeds at the word's first occurrence in the same text; analyze.py then prints a histogram of per-word speed-ratio buckets (slower, same, 2-2.99x, 3-3.99x, ... faster) against std::string::find and against libc strstr.

caveats: The 2-3x figure is a single README sentence matching analyze.py's '2.00 - 2.99 faster' bucket; no stored output, CPU, compiler version or libstdc++/glibc version, so it cannot be checked without running (the Makefile wgets i386.txt from an MIT course URL). The harness also times libc strstr (analyze.py and the README mislabel it 'strlen'), but no margin over strstr is claimed; strstr must also scan for the terminator while the SWAR routine gets the length. Timing is 10 iterations with microsecond gettimeofday and no warm-up, and words are taken from the searched text, so many searches end early and are timer-resolution noise. By code reading (not run), strstr64.cpp has correctness bugs: the SWAR zero-byte test can flag the byte above a real candidate through borrow, and memcmp checks only needle[1..k-1], so needle 'abb' in text 'a`bb' returns 1 instead of not-found; the loop 'i < n - k' with step 8 skips the last start position when n-k is a multiple of 8; and the 8-byte loads read up to 5 bytes past the string terminator. verify.cpp checks only words from the same text, so these cases are not exercised. The linked article 0x80.pl/articles/simd-friendly-karp-rabin.html was unreachable (DNS ENOTFOUND). last_commit is the last commit touching strstr/ (2016-01-17); the toys repo itself was last pushed 2026-04-08. name: WebAssembly memory.copy (bulk-memory-operations proposal)
baseline: Emscripten-generated wasm memcpy loop (aligned i32.load/i32.store) used in the Unity demo, plus manually unrolled i32 and i64 load/store loop variants
workload: Each row copies 1 GiB in total with a V8 prototype where memcpy/memmove exports are replaced by memory.copy, versus the wasm loops; copy sizes 32 B to 1 MiB within a 1 MiB working set.
claimed_speedup: At 128 KiB: memory.copy 29.728 Gib/s vs i64 load/store x4 10.032, i64 x2 7.934, i32 x2 3.975, plain i32 loop 2.782 Gib/s. At 1.0 KiB: 17.902 vs 7.010, 6.112, 3.568, 2.614 Gib/s. Loses at 32 B: intrinsic 1.382 vs i64 x4 1.565 Gib/s. At 1 MiB: 11.760 vs 10.091 Gib/s.
license: Per-directory (repo LICENSE): document/ W3C Software and Document Notice and License; interpreter/ and test/ Apache-2.0; papers/ CC-BY-4.0
stars_or_usage: 82 stars, 21 forks; archived Nov 3 2021; finished proposal merged into WebAssembly core spec 2.0 per WebAssembly/proposals finished-proposals.md
tradeoffs: A proposal text plus a hacked V8 prototype, not a library. The repo's LICENSE file points to per-directory licences (document/ under the W3C Software and Document Notice and License). The instruction itself is a runtime feature, so the benefit applies only to engines that call native MemMove for memory.copy.
caveats: Baseline is a 2017-era Emscripten wasm memcpy (gist c57dc945, memcpy.wast: byte prologue to 4-byte alignment, i32.load/i32.store word loop, byte tail; byte path when src and dst alignments differ) plus hand-unrolled variants, not a native libc memcpy; the prototype memory.copy simply called V8's native MemMove, so this is native memmove versus wasm-compiled loops. The benchmark gist (b8e8bc0c, memcpy.js, created 2017-10-26) is public, but its data initialisation and verification block is commented out, and the 'intrinsic' module's exported _memcpy body is a stub returning 0 that only the author's hacked V8 replaced with memory.copy, so the intrinsic column cannot be reproduced on a stock engine from the gist; the size-dependent curve (1.382 Gib/s at 32 B rising to 29.994 at 512 KiB, falling to 11.760 at 1 MiB) is consistent with real copying, not a no-op. Engine version, CPU model and flags are not given, and the stated 'L3 256k' looks mis-stated. Single first-party run. The repository is archived (2021-11-03); WebAssembly/proposals finished-proposals.md lists Bulk memory operations as finished and merged into core spec 2.0 (WG 2021-02-10), so memory.copy is now a standard instruction implemented by engines rather than a library.

The five newest commits (2026-07-14) are dependabot dependency bumps. Decode/disassembly throughput against other disassemblers, not assembly speed against GNU as, NASM or MASM (the category's spec baseline); objdump was not tested.

name: Intel XED (x86 encoder decoder)
baseline: Capstone (decode+format); Zydis and bddisasm (decode only)
workload: Decode-only and decode+format throughput in MB/s over the 77 MB x86-64 code section of Firefox 86.0.1 xul.dll, one shootout of nine x86 disassembler libraries.
claimed_speedup: icedland/disas-bench (2021, i5-6600K, gcc 10.3.0, LTO builds): decode only XED 55.39 MB/s vs Zydis 34.19 and bddisasm 35.48 MB/s (about 1.62x and 1.56x, derived from page data); decode+format XED 15.67 vs Capstone 14.02 MB/s (about 1.12x, derived from page data). The upstream athre0z/disas-bench charts (October 2025, no LTO, newer library versions) reverse the Capstone result: decode+format XED about 21 MB/s vs Capstone about 28 MB/s on a Ryzen 9 9950X (GCC 13.3) and about 20 vs 26 MB/s on an i9-13900K (GCC 14.2), so XED runs at about 0.76-0.77x of Capstone; decode only XED about 67 and 73 MB/s vs Zydis (full) about 50 and 57 MB/s (about 1.3x) but behind bddisasm (about 106 and 103 MB/s) and Zydis (min) (about 90 and 104 MB/s) (2025 values derived from page data: bar lengths read from the pixels of bench-amd.png and bench-intel.png against their axis ticks). hardware: Intel Core i5-6600K
tradeoffs: Intel's own IA32/Intel64 encoder and decoder library; built with a Python-based build system (mfile.py/mbuild); the benchmark builds it decoder-only. Other libraries in the same table are several times faster.
caveats: Weak and unstable win: the 2021 icedland run puts XED 1.12x ahead of Capstone in decode+format (derived), but the 2025 upstream athre0z/disas-bench runs on two newer CPUs put it about 0.77x of Capstone (slower), and bddisasm and Zydis (min) now decode faster than XED; only the decode-only lead over Zydis (full) holds in both runs (about 1.3-1.6x). XED sits mid-table or lower and is beaten by iced, yaxpeax and diStorm throughout. The 2021 shootout is run by the iced maintainers (a competitor) in a fork of athre0z/disas-bench; the 2025 runs are in the suite of a Zydis co-author; XED's own README makes no speed claim. The 2021 fork's bench/xed/main.c ignores xed_decode's error return (it formats and advances by the reported length even on invalid bytes); upstream later skips one byte per bad instruction and counts them. One timed run per library (one subprocess, clock() around the loop). Capstone cannot run decode-only, so no decode-only ratio against it. The 2021 build is decoder-only (mfile.py --no-encoder) with -flto; the 2025 build uses neither.

name: udis86
baseline: Zydis, bddisasm and Intel XED (decode only); it loses to Capstone and Zydis in decode+format
workload: Decode-only throughput in MB/s over the 77 MB x86-64 code section of Firefox 86.0.1 xul.dll in the disas-bench shootout of nine x86 disassembler libraries.

tradeoffs: Old, abandoned library; README lists MMX, x87, 3DNow, SSE through SSE4.2, AES, AMD-V, VMX and SMX and does not mention AVX or AVX-512, so it cannot decode current code; decoder tables are generated with Python scripts; slowest formatter in the shootout (12.02 MB/s decode+format, below BeaEngine's 13.42).

name: Minotaur
baseline: clang/LLVM -O3 without the Minotaur pass (per search snippets of the paper)
workload: Runtime of code compiled with and without the Minotaur LLVM pass: SPEC CPU 2017, the GMP benchmark suite and LibYUV.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract, seen via search snippets only (paper not opened): on an Intel Cascade Lake processor, GMP benchmark suite mean speedup 7.3% (max 13%) and SPEC CPU 2017 mean speedup 1.5% (max 4.5% on 638.imagick) over clang -O3. Single snippets also give a 1.2% SPEC mean on AMD and a LibYUV geomean of 1.029x on AMD Zen 3; a summary of an older paper version gives different LibYUV figures, so those two are unconfirmed.
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake (GMP and SPEC headline numbers); AMD Zen 3 for LibYUV and the compile-time tables per snippets; exact CPU models not seen
tradeoffs: Runs as an LLVM opt pass or via minotaur-cc / minotaur-c++ wrappers; needs a patched, RTTI- and EH-enabled LLVM build, Alive2, Z3 and Redis (offline cache mode), which makes the build heavy. Synthesis time adds to compile time.
caveats: All numbers come from search-result text of the paper (arXiv 2306.00229 v3, OOPSLA 2024); the paper, the NSF PAR copy, the deepai mirror and the 2022 LLVM Dev Meeting slides were all blocked, so methodology, flags and exact CPU models were not checked. The repo README has no performance numbers and no evaluation scripts (scripts/ holds only cache and compiler-wrapper tools). Gains on SPEC are small (1.2-1.5% mean). Per snippets, cold-cache builds can be hundreds of times slower than plain -O3 and warm-cache SPEC builds about 3% slower. Using it needs a patched LLVM (llvm-main-minotaur.patch) built with RTTI and exceptions, Alive2, Z3 and a redis server. It is an LLVM IR superoptimizer, so only loosely 'assembly tooling'.

name: STOKE
baseline: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 compiled x86-64 code (output quality); expert hand-written assembly for some kernels; Google Native Client's shipped libc string functions in the 2017 paper
workload: Runtime of superoptimized loop-free x86-64 kernels (OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication, Hacker's Delight, SAXPY, linked-list traversal) starting from llvm -O0 code, and 13 libc string functions from NaCl newlib.
claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2013 paper, Figure 1 caption and Section 1: the OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication kernel rewritten by STOKE is '16 lines shorter, 1.6x faster' than the gcc -O3 code 'and slightly faster than expert handwritten assembly'. Abstract: STOKE's programs 'either match or outperform the code produced by gcc -O3, icc -O3, and in some cases, expert handwritten assembly'. Figure 11 plots speedups over llvm -O0 for Hacker's Delight p01-p25, saxpy, mont and list; per-kernel values appear only in the chart. The README's popcount tutorial times a loop at 1.046 s for g++ -O3 -fno-inline versus 0.133 s after STOKE patches popcnt() (about 7.9x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 baselines (versions not stated in the extracted paper text); gcc-4.9 used in the 2017 paper's translation mode; README tutorial uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline
hardware: ASPLOS 2013: synthesis and optimization on a cluster of 40 dual-core 1.8 GHz AMD Opterons (machine used for the runtime speedups not identified in the extracted text); ASPLOS 2017: machines with two Intel Xeon E5-2667v2 3.3 GHz processors and 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and Intel-microarchitecture oriented. Needs test cases plus bounded or SMT-based equivalence checking, search budgets of tens of minutes per kernel on a cluster, and works best on short loop-free sequences. README: 'STOKE isn't production ready' and 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it says it is 'not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code'.
caveats: The paper is from 2013 and the speedups are on a small set of hand-picked loop-free kernels, plotted relative to llvm -O0 starting points in Figure 11; per-kernel numbers are chart-only, and the paper states no gcc/icc versions and does not name the timing machine. The README says 'We're not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code', calls STOKE a research prototype that 'isn't production ready', and says 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it needs gcc 4.9 to build. The README popcount tutorial's ~8x win compares against g++ -O3 without -march, so gcc cannot emit the popcnt instruction that STOKE uses; it shows the tool working, not a fair compiler comparison. The category fit (assembly tooling) is a judgement call: STOKE is a superoptimizer, and its baselines are compilers, not GNU as, NASM or MASM. The last commit (2020-12-04) only added a CodeQL workflow; the last code change is from 2019-10-03.

name: Unison
baseline: LLVM's register allocator and instruction scheduler (output quality, Hexagon, ARM and MIPS back ends)
workload: Estimated speedup and code size of functions from MediaBench and SPEC CPU2006 compiled with Unison's integrated combinatorial register allocation and instruction scheduling versus LLVM.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (arXiv 1804.02452 abstract via WebSearch; paper not opened): mean estimated speedup over LLVM from 1.1% to 10% and mean code size reduction from 1.3% to 3.8% depending on the architecture (code size: MIPS 3.8%, ARM 2.5%, Hexagon 1.3%, where LLVM's heuristics are already near-optimal for size), on functions from MediaBench and SPEC CPU2006. The authors report that running the generated code on Hexagon confirms that the estimated speedup becomes actual speedup.
hardware: Hexagon (execution check); estimates for ARM and MIPS
tradeoffs: Haskell tool driving constraint solvers, used through a Unison-enabled LLVM fork (github.com/unison-code/llvm); solving time is far higher than LLVM's heuristics; targets Hexagon, ARM and MIPS rather than x86.
caveats: Numbers are 'estimated' speedups from a static cost model, not measured runtimes, except for the Hexagon execution check. The metric is the quality of the generated code: Unison's constraint solving is far slower than LLVM's heuristic register allocator and scheduler, and the paper describes scaling to medium-sized functions of up to about 1,000 instructions, so compile time is a cost, not a win. The repo README and project site (unison-code.github.io index.md, checked via raw.githubusercontent.com) make no performance claims and link no results; the paper (arXiv 1804.02452, TOPLAS doi 10.1145/3332373), the project site's publication pages and the Ericsson research blog 'Outperforming state-of-the-art compilers with Unison' were unreachable here, so all numbers are from search-result text. Needs an LLVM fork (unison-code/llvm) as a driver. Last commit 2023-01-15 (abandoned). Filed under assemblers-and-asm-tooling, though it is really a compiler back-end component (register allocation and instruction scheduling).

name: aron
baseline: macOS as (the system assembler on macOS, not GNU as)
workload: Assembling the repo's test.macos.s, a 31-line clang -S (Intel syntax) output of a hello-world printf program, once per process, with aron versus the macOS assembler; timings are dominated by process startup.
claimed_speedup: README screenshot (imgs/aron-bm.png) of 'hyperfine -N --warmup 10 "target/release/aron test.macos.s" "as test.macos.s"': aron 3.9 ms +/- 0.7 ms (777 runs) versus as 49.8 ms +/- 2.3 ms (60 runs), summary 'aron ... ran 12.94 +/- 2.34 times faster than as'. The README introduces it with 'This is not empirical by any means'.
compiler_and_flags: aron built with cargo release profile (target/release); the screenshot's shell prompt shows rust v1.60.0 and C v13.1.6-clang (Apple clang 13.1.6 toolchain, which supplies the baseline as), aron v0.1.0; timed with hyperfine -N --warmup 10. No other flags stated.
hardware: A macOS machine; CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Incomplete x86-64 assembler (README says so); outputs ELF and Mach-O objects; supports only part of the instruction set and directives, so it cannot replace GNU as, NASM or MASM on general input.
caveats: The README says 'This is not empirical by any means'. One 31-line hello-world input (about 15 instructions), so both timings measure process launch rather than assembly: aron finishes in 3.9 ms while macOS as, a driver that hands off to clang's integrated assembler, takes 49.8 ms mostly in startup. No CPU is named, the output objects are not compared, and the assembler is self-described as incomplete, so the speedup also reflects its narrower feature set. The baseline is macOS as, not GNU as. The screenshot was taken on aron v0.1.0 (August 2022); the repo is now at 0.2.0. The language is Rust (Cargo.toml, edition 2021) although the repo page shows no language bar.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'assembler faster than GNU as NASM benchmark assemble time github'

verification.tier_reason: The only number is a README screenshot (imgs/aron-bm.png) of hyperfine -N --warmup 10 assembling test.macos.s, a 31-line clang -S output of a hello-world printf program: aron 3.9 ms vs macOS as 49.8 ms, 12.94 +/- 2.34x. With ~15 instructions of input both timings are process launch (macOS as is a driver that hands off to clang's integrated assembler), so the figure says nothing about assembly speed; the author calls it 'not empirical by any means', no CPU is named, and no output equivalence is checked. Downgraded to D following the wave 11 hop precedent (startup-dominated benchmark); it would be C on the bare rubric.

Shortcomings: startup-dominated hello-world benchmark (31-line file), author disclaims it as not empirical, CPU unstated, no output check, incomplete assembler, 2 stars, abandoned since 2022-10-11. name: Asmc
baseline: MASM (Microsoft Macro Assembler 6.15 and 10.0), also compared with JWasm and UASM
workload: Assemble time of a 21,000-line MASM-syntax source in a forum user's test.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: in a masm32.com thread (msg=92718) jj2007 timed a 21,000-line source at 1200 ms for AsmC versus 1800 ms for MASM 6.15 and 10.0 (1.5x, derived from snippet data), 1480 ms JWasm and 1630 ms UAsm64. A 2021 post by the same user (msg=102515) times a full build of the 22k+ line RichMasm source at 1259 ms with AsmC versus 2185 ms with ML 10.0 (about 1.7x, derived from snippet data) and 1688 ms with UAsm64, for 32-bit code. Another poster (msg=129297) says UAsm is about 25% slower than AsmC. The README makes no speed claim.
tradeoffs: Written in assembly (MASM syntax, self-hosted); runs on Windows and Linux; GPL licence; MASM compatibility is not perfect (the project adds its own macro/language extensions and claims MASM v14 AVX-512 support while its Version macro is v10).
caveats: The MASM-compatible assembler timing numbers appear only in a WebSearch result snippet of a masm32.com forum thread (page unreachable here: ENOTFOUND), recorded as 'snippet only'; the same thread says on a 21,000-line source MASM 6.15 and 10.0 took 1800 ms each, UAsm64 1630 ms, JWasm 1480 ms and AsmC 1200 ms. Anecdotal forum measurement, no hardware, flags or versions seen. One poster in the same snippet says the same extensions make him distrust the tool, and another snippet claim of a '7-8x' speed-up over MASM contradicts the 1.5x timing above.

name: MaxAs
baseline: cuBLAS sgemm (NVIDIA's library kernels, compiled by NVIDIA's toolchain)
workload: Hand-scheduled single-precision GEMM kernels written in Maxwell SASS and assembled with MaxAs, versus cuBLAS sgemm, on large (4096) and small matrices.
claimed_speedup: SGEMM walkthrough: 'performing as much as 25% over cublas' for small matrices (64-thread version) and 'beating cublas by 4.8%' at size 4096 (256-thread version); about 98% of theoretical peak on GM107 and 96% on GM204. Absolute GFLOPS appear only in chart images.
hardware: NVIDIA GM204 (Maxwell) at a sustained 1607 MHz core clock (1620 MHz boost scores excluded) with 8000 MHz memory; GM107 also cited for the 98% efficiency figure. Card model, driver, CUDA and cuBLAS versions are not stated on the page.
tradeoffs: Assembler for NVIDIA Maxwell SASS only (GTX 9xx era), written in Perl; the repository is archived and Intel has discontinued the project. Gains come from hand-written kernels and scheduling, not from the assembler alone.
caveats: First-party wiki claim; exact per-size GFLOPS are only in chart images, and the page names no cuBLAS, CUDA or driver version, no card model and no flags. The public harness (sgemm/sgemm.cpp with sgemm.pl, a Windows Visual Studio build) has its cuBLAS timing code commented out, so the comparison cannot be rerun as published. The author says the kernels were 'derived from detailed study of the cublas Kepler and Maxwell sgemm implementations', and part of the gap comes from a cuBLAS bug that the wiki says costs cuBLAS sgemm 28 GFLOPS on GM204; the 2015-era cuBLAS has long since been superseded. The speedup is of a hand-scheduled SASS kernel against a library, not of the assembler against ptxas, GNU as, NASM or MASM; MaxAs only targets Maxwell (later partial half and dp4a support). Archived by the owner on 2023-01-03 with an Intel discontinuation notice; the last code commit is from 2016-06-10. Treat as a reference, not a general assembler win.
found_via: GitHub: README and SGEMM wiki page of NervanaSystems/maxas, found while looking for GPU (SASS) assemblers

verification.tier_reason: First-party SGEMM wiki states 'as much as 25% over cublas' for small matrices (64-thread kernel) and 'At the 4096 size we're beating cublas by 4.8%' (256-thread kernel), 98% of theoretical on GM107 and 96% on GM204; GFLOPS exist only in chart images. The harness (sgemm/sgemm.cpp, sgemm.pl) is public but its cuBLAS timing calls are commented out, it builds as a Windows Visual Studio project, and no CUDA, cuBLAS or driver version or card model is given, so not A; no independent head-to-head found (maxDNN arXiv 1501.06633 reports 96% efficiency for a maxas-style SGEMM, snippet only, no cuBLAS comparison).
verification.notes: Wiki numbers match the record (25% small-matrix, 4.8% at 4096, 98%/96% efficiency). Shortcomings: first-party, GFLOPS chart-only, no cuBLAS/CUDA versions or card model, cuBLAS comparison code commented out in the published harness, kernels derived from cuBLAS's own SASS plus a cuBLAS bug, archived 2023 (last code 2016).

name: SuperCoder
baseline: gcc -O3 compiled assembly (output quality)
workload: Runtime speedup of LLM-rewritten x86 assembly versus the gcc -O3 assembly on a benchmark of 8,072 real-world programs averaging 130 lines (CodeNet-derived), with test-based correctness checks.
claimed_speedup: Per WebSearch result text of arXiv 2505.11480 only (paper not opened): the RL-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct model reaches a 95.0% test pass rate and a 1.46x average speedup over gcc -O3; the strongest baseline LLM (Claude-opus-4) reaches 51.5% pass rate and 1.43x average speedup.
compiler_and_flags: Per the paper (snippet only): baseline assembly from gcc -O3. Released scripts: src/create_data/convert_to_hf_raw.py emits gcc -O0 -S (stored as 'unoptimized_assembly', the prompt input and the timing baseline) and gcc -O3 -S (stored as the reference answer); all assembly is linked with plain 'gcc file.s -o bin -lm'; gcc version not stated. Timing: hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 10, mean whole-process wall time per test input, up to 10 inputs per program.
stars_or_usage: 2 stars, 0 forks; model weights published as LLM4Code/Superoptimizer_Qwen7B on HuggingFace
tradeoffs: Probabilistic output: correctness is test-based (95.0% pass rate, not formal equivalence), so rewrites need independent verification. Needs a GPU-capable RL setup (verl) to retrain; model weights and dataset are listed on Hugging Face in the README.
caveats: Headline numbers come from WebSearch snippets of arXiv 2505.11480 (paper not opened; arXiv and alphaXiv blocked); the README has no results section and states no hardware or gcc version. The released harness (src/test_benchmark.py) floors every per-input speedup at 1.0 ('If generated code is slower, set speedup to 1.0'), gives failed, non-compiling or benchmark-failing cases a speedup of 1.0 (they are averaged in as 1.0, not excluded), and treats output identical to the baseline assembly as correct at 1.0 without running it, so the reported average can never fall below 1.0 and is biased upward. In the released dataset-building scripts (src/create_data/convert_to_hf_raw.py, create_top_speedup.py) the 'unoptimized_assembly' that test_benchmark.py times against is gcc -O0 output, while the paper says the baseline is gcc -O3; the published HuggingFace dataset (LLM4Code/llm_superoptimizer_ds) could not be opened to check which variant the reported numbers used, so the repo as released does not demonstrably reproduce the -O3 comparison. Correctness is checked on at most 10 CodeNet test inputs per program, and timings are whole-process (startup included) on small competitive-programming programs, run concurrently in a thread pool. The output is a fine-tuned model (HuggingFace LLM4Code/Superoptimizer_Qwen7B, licence not checked), not a library; the repo is a 2-commit code drop. Preprint status.

verification.notes: Repo, Apache-2.0 licence, 2 stars and last commit 2025-10-23 (2 commits, both that day) confirmed on github.com; still 'active' until 2026-10-23. Shortcomings to record: speedup floored at 1.0 per input and failures averaged in as 1.0 (record's caveat said failures were excluded; corrected), released scripts time against gcc -O0 assembly while the paper claims gcc -O3 (unresolved, HF dataset unreachable), no CPU or gcc version, preprint numbers seen only in search snippets. Not invalid evidence, so kept at C.

name: Fadec
baseline: libopcodes, Capstone and Zydis (x86 decoding libraries)
workload: Decoding x86-32 and x86-64 instructions with a lookup-table decoder; a separate x86-64 encoder is included.
claimed_speedup: 'Fadec is significantly faster than libopcodes, Capstone, or Zydis due to the absence of high-level abstractions and the small lookup table' (no numbers); encoder API v2 'about 3x faster than v1' (internal comparison).
stars_or_usage: 235 stars, 33 forks, 432 commits (github.com page, 2026-10-11). Used as a git submodule (deps/fadec) by the TPDE compiler back-end framework (tpde2/tpde .gitmodules, opened). Search results also show copies at android.googlesource.com platform/external/lfi/fadec (tagged android-17.0.0_r1) and a Chromium mirror chromium.googlesource.com/external/github.com/aengelke/fadec, plus forks oleavr/fadec and GenKyoko/fadec (snippet only; googlesource host did not resolve here).
tradeoffs: C library with no dependencies, about 95 KiB with decoder and encoder, usable in freestanding environments. Targets Intel 64 behaviour; AMD-specific differences are not handled. Decoded operand sizes are not always exact for speed.
caveats: No benchmark numbers or comparison harness anywhere: the speed claim over libopcodes, Capstone and Zydis is qualitative, and the only timing tool in the repo (decode-profile.c, added 2026-06-01) measures Fadec alone. Fadec is absent from the public disas-bench candidate lists (athre0z and iximeow forks). The encoder v2 '3x faster than v1' figure is an internal comparison with no baseline and comes at ~3 MiB code size (off by default, -Dwith_encode2=true). README lists known issues: low test coverage, register-uniqueness constraints not enforced (VSIB, AMX, AVX-512 FP16 complex multiply), decoded operand sizes not always exact, AMD64-specific behaviour not handled (Intel 64 semantics only), MPX, HLE, XOP, FMA4 and Xeon Phi unsupported. name: SLOTHY
baseline: unscheduled 'clean' hand-written assembly and prior hand-optimized implementations of the same kernels (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs, FFT, X25519); no compiler baseline stated on the pages opened
workload: Instruction scheduling, register allocation and software pipelining of hand-written Arm AArch64, Armv8.1-M and RISC-V assembly for cryptographic and DSP kernels.
claimed_speedup: README: SLOTHY has been used 'to provide the fastest known implementations of various cryptographic and DSP primitives' (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs for Cortex-A55/A72/M55/M85, FFT for Cortex-M55/M85, X25519 for Cortex-A55); no speedup numbers on any page opened. Related adoption number: the AWS-LC pull request that imported the s2n-bignum X25519 rewrite (partly SLOTHY-generated) reports 12867.1 to 22361.9 ops/sec ('74% speedup') on Graviton 2, but that gain is not attributable to SLOTHY alone.
hardware: Targets Cortex-M55, M85, A55 (supported), A72, Cortex-X/Neoverse-V, Apple M1 (experimental) and XuanTie C908
stars_or_usage: 352 stars; adopted in AWS-LC / s2n-bignum, Arm EndpointAI CMSIS DSP and mlkem-native
tradeoffs: Microarchitecture-specific by design: each output is scheduled for one core model (portability note: code tuned for Cortex-A55 is not tuned for other cores). Solver time is seconds to minutes for under 50 instructions and minutes to hours for up to 150 instructions; larger kernels need heuristics. Python tool using Google OR-Tools.
caveats: The TCHES 2024 paper 'Fast and Clean: Auditable high-performance assembly via constraint solving' (issue 1, pp. 87-132, artifact at artifacts.iacr.org/tches/2024/a6; eprint 2022/1303) is peer-reviewed but could not be opened (tches.iacr.org and eprint unreachable); WebSearch snippets only say the SLOTHY-optimized code matches or beats prior art in all cases, with no cycle counts. The repo ships clean and optimized sources (paper/clean, paper/opt), optimization scripts (paper/scripts) and a Docker artifact; cycle benchmarks live in pqax/pqmx and need Cortex-A55/A72 devices or an MPS3 FPGA board (AN547/AN555), and builds without CYCLES=PMU/PERF stub out cycle counts. The only number in the repo is the tutorial's LLVM-MCA model estimate for a toy Cortex-A55 loop (31 to 21 cycles per iteration), a model output against its own unscheduled input, not a measurement. Adoption is real: s2n-bignum PR #108 (merged 2024-02-15) imported the SLOTHY-generated Lenngren-based X25519 without benchmark numbers; the AWS-LC PR #1469 that reports 12867.1 to 22361.9 ops/sec ('74% speedup', Graviton 2) was closed without merge on 2024-03-06 (the README calls it merged) and mixes the algorithm change with SLOTHY scheduling. CP-SAT is non-deterministic, so re-optimization results vary, especially for the heuristic Cortex-A72 model. SLOTHY is a Python tool that produces assembly; it is not linked into the user's program.

language: Almide (statically typed language compiling to Rust and WebAssembly)
baseline: Ordinary hand-written Rust (Box-linked recursive enum, no arena, rustc 1.96.1 opt-level=3, LTO, 1 codegen unit)
workload: Benchmarks-Game-style programs (binarytrees, treealloc, n-body, spectral-norm, fasta, FFT) on native output; wasm output measured as a ratio to native
claimed_speedup: Native output vs ordinary hand-written Rust on Apple M4 Pro (almide 0.62.0, 2026-09-08, median of 9 interleaved runs): binarytrees d17 134 ms vs 382 ms (0.35x time), d19 581 vs 1826 ms (0.32x); treealloc d20 112 vs 375 ms (0.30x), d21 221 vs 748 ms (0.30x). With the region window turned off (ALMIDE_REGION_OFF=1) the same Almide source is 1.10-1.26x slower than the Rust reference. ubuntu-latest CI runner (2026-10-03, almide 0.66.0 dev): binarytrees 0.581 (d17), treealloc 0.365 (d20). Arithmetic kernels (2026-07-30, rustc 1.96.1): n-body and spectral-norm 1.00x, fasta 1.16x and FFT 1.18x slower than Rust. Wasm leg: README ledger (2026-09-29, embedded wasm host vs native binary, min of 2x5 interleaved) gives wasm/native ratios of 0.67x (mapbuild) to 1.96x (listbuild_append), e.g. treealloc 1.04x, binarytrees 1.07x, nbody 1.10x, fft 1.53x; these ratios are on the README, not on BENCHMARKS.md, whose older dated wasm paragraph still describes FFT (~3,500x) and mandelbrot (~130x) cliffs.
compiler_and_flags: almide --release (emits Rust, cargo release profile opt-level=3 + LTO) vs handwritten Rust built by bench.py with rustc -C opt-level=3 -C lto=yes -C codegen-units=1; median of 9 interleaved runs after warmup; byte-identical stdout verified before timing. rustc 1.96.1 is stated for the 2026-07-30 scoreboard; the 2026-09-08 victory JSON records almide 0.62.0 but no rustc version (README says CI builds with 1.96.0).
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (arm64), almide 0.62.0, 2026-09-08; also an ubuntu-latest CI runner
tradeoffs: Young language optimised for LLM code generation; wins on allocation-heavy rows come from a compiler-proven region (bump-arena) window the ordinary Rust program does not have. Loses on fasta and FFT.
caveats: Off the category baseline: the comparison is native Rust output, not TypeScript/JS in V8 or C++ via Emscripten, and the wasm output is only compared with Almide's own native binary, never with JS/V8 or an Emscripten build. The whole win is one optimization (the region window, a thread-local bump arena rewound once per check(make(d)) tree) against a Rust reference that deliberately pays malloc/free per Box node; a Rust program using an arena (bumpalo/typed-arena, as Benchmarks Game Rust entries do) would close most of the gap (the same document shows a Zig arena at 88 ms vs Almide 72 ms at d16). The README's third victory row (fannkuchredux 0.21/0.12 via parallel fan) compares a threaded Almide run with a one-thread Rust reference and should not be cited. Self-reported by the project.

name: json-as
baseline: JavaScript built-in JSON.parse / JSON.stringify in V8 (also fast-json-parse and assemblyscript-json)
workload: End-to-end JSON deserialize (including allocating the destination object) and serialize throughput in MB/s on small payloads (19 B to 5.5 kB) and nine standard payloads from the yyjson and nativejson-benchmark corpora, with json-as compiled to Wasm by the AssemblyScript compiler (asc) and run in V8.
claimed_speedup: Deserialize, SWAR mode vs built-in JSON in V8: 1,321 vs 568 MB/s (1.1 kB payload), 5,734 vs 1,295 MB/s (5.5 kB payload), 2,196 vs 168 MB/s (108 B payload), 1,056 vs 401 MB/s (52 B alphabet string). Serialize, SIMD mode vs built-in JSON: 7,775 vs 1,062 MB/s (5.5 kB payload), 3,818 vs 696 MB/s (1.1 kB payload). Library comparison on a 5 KiB GitHub-repo payload (deserialize): json-as struct 5,636 MB/s, native JSON 547 MB/s, fast-json-parse 547 MB/s, assemblyscript-json 32 MB/s. Smallest-gain row: 3D Vector (19 B) deserialize, 356-444 vs 83 MB/s across the three typed modes, while the dynamic JSON.Obj path ties built-in JSON on that row (82 vs 83 MB/s). Numbers read from the chart images overview-deserialize.png, overview-serialize.png and library-deserialize.png on the docs branch (v1.5.0).
tradeoffs: Typed, schema-driven (struct) API: the build-time transform generates a specialised serializer per @json class, so it only competes with JSON.parse when the schema is known up front; dynamic JSON.Obj path is slower. Needs AssemblyScript toolchain and a Wasm host; builds use --noAssert and --uncheckedBehavior always, which removes bounds and assert checks. SIMD mode needs Wasm SIMD support.
caveats: First-party: the benchmark author is the library author. Chart values exist only in images (SVG and PNG on the docs branch, charts/v1.5.0), not in a text table. The JS baseline parses into generic JavaScript objects while json-as parses into typed structs generated at build time, so the work differs. Harness asymmetry: the JS blackbox() in bench/lib/bench.js runs an indirect eval of '%PerformMicrotaskCheckpoint();' on every timed op, while the AS blackbox is a single store/load, which inflates JS per-op time most on the 19-108 byte rows (JS ops there take only about 125-640 ns); the 5.5 kB rows are least affected. Benchmark builds use --noAssert, --uncheckedBehavior always and wasm-opt -tnh/-iit, which drop assertion and trap checks. The JSON.Obj path is lazy by default since v1.5.0 (values parsed on first access, untouched values re-serialized by copying source bytes), so its deserialize and serialize bars (up to 19,968 MB/s) defer work and are not like-for-like; on the 3D Vector row JSON.Obj ties built-in JSON (82 vs 83 MB/s), and the 0 values on the Alphabet and UUIDv4 rows mean no JSON.Obj run, not a loss. In the library chart fast-json-parse wraps JSON.parse, which is why it equals native JSON (547 MB/s). The SIMD mode is slower than SWAR on several deserialize rows (Small Payload 1,089 vs 2,196 MB/s). A key-matching correctness bug (final UTF-16 unit of odd-length keys longer than 4 units not compared) was fixed on 2026-10-04 (PR #223), after the charted run; the fix is in toMemCCheck/toMemCDecl, which only the generated __DESERIALIZE_SLOW fallback uses, and the AS large bench asserts a byte-exact round trip, so the charted fast-path numbers are not capped by it. baseline: JavaScript image filter in the browser; also Rust compiled to WASM ('Rust Native' row)
workload: Browser demo (examples/wasm_filter/www/index.html): one call of an RGBA filter (invert, grayscale or brightness; the README table does not say which) on a user-uploaded 2.1 MB image, timed with performance.now around a single call with no warm-up or repetition; the wasm rows include wasm-bindgen copy-in and copy-out of the Vec<u8>, the JS row allocates a new Uint8Array

Each figure is one click timed with performance.now, quantized to 0.1 ms. The example README (examples/wasm_filter/README.md) carries a different table for a 1920x1080 8.3 MB image (Zig WASM ~5 ms, pure JS ~25 ms, 'Canvas API' ~15 ms for invert) with a Canvas API row that has no implementation in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: Zig -O ReleaseFast -mcpu=mvp+simd128 -fno-stack-protector, target wasm32-freestanding (engine/src/zig_compiler.rs; the example README still says ReleaseSmall); Rust wasm32-unknown-unknown with opt-level "s", lto = true and -C target-feature=+simd128 (examples/wasm_filter/Cargo.toml, .cargo/config.toml), built with wasm-pack --target web; browser and JS engine not stated
tradeoffs: Combines Rust (memory and wasm-bindgen glue) with Zig compute kernels in one .wasm; needs the Zig toolchain at build time.
caveats: Single-sample browser timings (one click, no warm-up, 0.1 ms timer granularity); browser, hardware and which filter was timed are not stated. The Zig SIMD invert_colors_raw subtracts every byte from 255, including alpha, while the Rust and JS versions and the example README ('Alpha channel unchanged') leave alpha intact, so the timed fast path produces different output (opaque pixels become transparent); the SIMD brightness path likewise changes alpha for negative deltas. A correct masked SIMD version would cost about the same, so the bug does not obviously create the speedup, but the row does not time the specified filter. The 'Rust native' baseline is a bounds-checked scalar step_by(4) loop built at opt-level "s" (size), so the 3x over Rust measures hand-written SIMD128 against a size-optimized scalar loop, not Zig against Rust; the grayscale filter is scalar in Zig too. The example README's second table (8.3 MB, ~5 vs ~25 ms, Canvas API row) has no matching code and looks unmeasured. Trivially vectorizable byte filter; crate autozig 0.1.2 with 80 downloads (crates.io, 14 recent); 5 stars; first-party only.

name: ademakov/bzero
language: Assembly (x86 SSE/AVX, GNU as) with C test harness
baseline: libc memset (bzero_0 in the harness) and the author's trivial and unrolled C versions compiled with gcc -O2
workload: Time to clear buffers of 0 to 2048+ bytes by size, comparing libc memset, trivial/unrolled C, SSE intrinsics, rep stosb, and hand-written SSE/AVX assembly versions.
claimed_speedup: Core i7-4850HQ (total microseconds for 10,000 calls): 32 B bzero_6 26 / bzero_7 23 vs memset 86 (3.3x / 3.7x, derived from page data); 64 B 26 vs 70 (2.7x, derived from page data); 256 B 51 vs 82 (1.6x, derived from page data); 1024 B 189 vs 149 and 2048 B 393 vs 241 (memset faster). Xeon E5520 (no AVX): 64 B 47 vs 71, 256 B 79 vs 127, 1024 B 265 vs 317, 2048 B bzero_6 655 / bzero_7 552 vs memset 664. The README Update says newer AVX versions (bzero_9..bzero_H, added 2019) are 'faster than memset() for any memory size', but no tables or numbers are given for them.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (version not stated). Published flags unclear: the 2017 Makefile (commit e807b1d) sets only CC=gcc with no CFLAGS (gcc default -O0); the current Makefile sets CFLAGS=-march=native with no -O level; the README says only 'gcc -O2' gives naive C results and that clang -O2 or gcc -O3 may rewrite the C versions into memset. The assembly versions do not depend on the -O level.
hardware: Intel Xeon E5520 @ 2.27 GHz (no AVX) and Intel Core i7-4850HQ @ 2.30 GHz (AVX)
tradeoffs: Strong only for small sizes and the SSE versions; the author concludes stock memset is better for large buffers when it can use AVX/AVX2. Public-domain dedication gives no patent grant.
caveats: Units derived from main.c: each figure is the total gettimeofday time in microseconds for 10,000 calls on the same buffer (so 23 vs 26 is within 1 us timer noise; about 2.3-2.6 ns per call); one run per size, hot cache, same size every call (branch-friendly). Published tables come from the 2017 harness (the current main.c prints a different size list) on 2009/2013 CPUs with an unstated glibc; author notes stock memset is 'sometimes unreasonably bad for small buffer sizes' there, which modern glibc ERMS/AVX2/EVEX memset paths likely fixed. name: CryptOpt
baseline: GCC 12.1.0 and Clang 15.0.6 compiling Fiat Cryptography's generated C at -O3 -march=native -mtune=native; also hand-optimized assembly (OpenSSL fe-51/fe-64, libsecp256k1 asm, HACL* fe-64)
metric: latency (CPU cycles per finite-field multiply and square)
workload: Multiply and square in nine prime fields (Curve25519, NIST P-224/P-256/P-384/P-521, secp256k1, Curve448, SIKEp434 field, Poly1305) on ten x86-64 CPUs, plus scalar multiplication through SUPERCOP.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: mean speedup 1.74 over GCC 12.1.0 and 1.40 over Clang 15.0.6 across ten x86-64 platforms; 1.04 average speedup over the hand-optimized assembly in libsecp256k1. Table 4 geometric means of CryptOpt over Clang / GCC, Mul: Curve25519 1.25/1.16, P-224 1.54/2.52, P-256 1.70/2.61, P-384 1.45/2.49, SIKEp434 1.70/2.43, Curve448 1.19/0.98, P-521 1.30/0.97, Poly1305 1.12/1.22, secp256k1 1.80/2.62.
compiler_and_flags: Baseline C built with GCC 12.1.0 and Clang 15.0.6, highest optimization level with -march=native -mtune=native -O3; CPU frequency fixed, boosting disabled, performance governor; Ubuntu Server 22.04.1.
hardware: Ten x86-64 machines: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 1900X (Zen 1), Ryzen 7 5800X and Ryzen 9 5950X (Zen 3), Ryzen 9 7950X (Zen 4); Intel Core i7-6770HQ, i7-10710U, i9-10900K, i7-11700KF, i9-12900KF, i9-13900KF (performance cores only).
stars_or_usage: 73 stars, 14 forks; PLDI 2023 Distinguished Paper Award and GECCO 2023 Humies Gold award (university news pages, snippet only); verified assembly published in fiat-crypto's fiat-amd64 directory and Curve25519 code integrated into BoringSSL (per the repo README)
tradeoffs: x86-64 only; the assembly is found by randomized search per microarchitecture (20 to 40 wall-clock hours per machine for the 18 primitives) and must be regenerated for new CPUs; correctness is checked by an equivalence checker only when the input is Fiat IR, the libsecp256k1 variant is unverified; fixed-size field arithmetic, not a general library.
caveats: The assembly is machine-generated by random program search, not hand-written; it sits here because it is compared against both compilers and hand-written assembly. Each platform's numbers come from code optimized on and for that same platform (best of three optimization runs per primitive per machine), against generic compiler output. Gains vary: Curve448 and P-521 multiply are slightly slower than GCC (0.98 and 0.97); gains are modest for Curve25519 and Poly1305. The baseline is Fiat Cryptography's generated C, not each library's own C. In whole scalar multiplication through SUPERCOP (Table 5, geometric-mean cycles) CryptOpt-enhanced code is on par with OpenSSL fe-51 (524k vs 530k) and fe-64 (461k vs 455k) assembly and slower than HACL* fe-64 (452k); for secp256k1, libsecp256k1's hand asm (547k) is itself slower than its portable C (530k), so CryptOpt's 527k (Fiat, verified) and 528k (Opt) are under 1 percent faster than libsecp256k1's C (derived from page data), and the 1.04 speedup over hand asm comes from the libsecp256k1-derived path that the equivalence checker cannot verify. The Zenodo artifact was not opened (blocked here); the repo README repeats the Table 4 means. Last commit 2023-11-16.

name: memcpy_benchmark (AVX-256, AVX-512 and rep movsb NASM memcpy)
baseline: libc built-in memcpy (glibc version not stated)
workload: Single-threaded copy of one large buffer per run (512 MiB when result.txt was recorded on 2020-09-20; the current code uses 128 MiB), 11 runs per routine; each run mallocs a fresh source (memset before timing) and a fresh, untouched destination, times one copy with gettimeofday, then checks it with memcmp. Routines: libc memcpy, NASM AVX-256 and AVX-512 unrolled copies with prefetcht1, and a three-instruction rep movsb. The multithreaded mode (option 5, libs/memcpy_multithread.c) was added later and is not in result.txt.
claimed_speedup: result.txt, seconds per copy of one 512 MiB buffer (MEM_ALLOC at the result commit; units from memcpy_bench.c's printf), lower is better. Xeon Platinum 8269CY: libc memcpy min 0.3494 / avg 0.3853 vs AVX-256 asm min 0.2711 / avg 0.2987 (about 1.29x), AVX-512 asm min 0.2854 / avg 0.3150 (about 1.22x), rep movsb min 0.3020 / avg 0.3333 (about 1.16x). AMD A8-6410: libc min 0.5464 / avg 0.6221 vs AVX asm min 0.4471 / avg 0.4967 (about 1.22-1.25x) and plain rep movsb min 0.4450 / avg 0.4970 (about 1.23-1.25x); AVX-512 not supported. Ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: gcc at the time of the results (Makefile switched to cc on 2020-09-21) with -Wall -ggdb3 -fPIC -fpic -O3 for the C harness; nasm -felf64 for the assembly; compiler, NASM and glibc versions not stated (the baseline memcpy is the prebuilt libc routine, so the C flags do not affect it)
hardware: AMD A8-6410 APU (2 GHz, no AVX-512) and Intel Xeon Platinum 8269CY (2.5 GHz; cpuinfo flags include 'hypervisor', so a cloud VM); README tells users to set the performance governor, not confirmed for these runs
tradeoffs: x86-64 only; AVX-512 variant needs AVX-512 (reported 'CPU is not supported' on the AMD A8); rep movsb performance depends on ERMS/FSRM support; routines are plain memcpy without small-size dispatch.
caveats: Author's own runs; the README makes no speed claim. Harness flaws: the loop runs TEST_COUNT+1 = 11 copies but divides the total by 10, so every reported Avg exceeds its Max (Xeon libc Avg 0.3853 vs Max 0.3533); ratios survive because all routines share the bug. The destination is a fresh 512 MiB malloc (mmap) never touched before timing, so each timed copy includes about 131,072 first-touch page faults; derived copy rates of about 0.9-2.0 GB/s are well below memory bandwidth, so the numbers mix fault cost with copy speed and may reflect how each store pattern interacts with faulting rather than kernel efficiency. On the A8 the plain rep movsb routine matches the AVX routine, so the gain there is not from the AVX kernel. AVX-512 is slower than AVX-256 on the Xeon. glibc version (which selects the memcpy variant and its non-temporal threshold), compiler and NASM versions are unknown; one result set per machine. The current code uses a 128 MiB buffer, so rerunning it does not reproduce the recorded configuration. The asm measured equals today's libs/memcpy_avx256.asm (only a comment changed).

name: asmlib (abiiranathan)
language: Assembly (NASM x86-64 AVX2/BMI2; GNU as AArch64 NEON) with a C header and a portable C/wasm backend
baseline: glibc 2.44 memcpy/memset/memcmp/strlen/memchr/strstr/memmem, malloc/free, snprintf, sscanf and libm
workload: Nanoseconds per call from micro-benchmarks (bench/*.c) of asm_* routines against the glibc versions, best of 7 to 9 trials; function pointers are held volatile so the compiler cannot inline libc builtins.
claimed_speedup: docs/BENCHMARKS.md (glibc 2.44, i7-10510U, best of 7-9): arena 4.36 vs 37.46 ns/op (8.59x), arena mixed 8..512B 19.80x, 2048 x 1 KiB fill+release 22.28 vs 1012.72 us (45.46x); asm_malloc heap 4.79x (1000 x 64B) and 8.08x (mixed); asm_sscanf 2.18-3.05x (sscanf %d 130.93 vs 44.78 ns, 2.92x); asm_snprintf 1.53-2.10x (mixed 159.32 vs 104.35 ns) and asm_u64toa 20.32 ns vs snprintf %llu 80.79 ns (3.98x); libm: cbrt 2.18x, asinh 1.38x, cosh 1.33x, sqrt and atan2 1.02x, the other 13 functions 0.52-0.99x (sinh 0.52x). Memory/string results are given only as README ranges: memchr about 1.1-1.2x from 128 B up, mid/large memcpy/memset/memcmp 0.95-1.2x, strlen 0.5-0.8x and strstr 0.4-0.65x (glibc faster); 'memmem is several times faster' has no benchmark (bench/bench.c does not time memmem).
compiler_and_flags: Harnesses built by the Makefile with $(CC) and CFLAGS -O2 -Wall -Wextra (math_bench: -O2 -fno-builtin, math objects -O2 -ffreestanding -fno-builtin -ffp-contract=off); assembly via NASM. docs/BENCHMARKS.md lists GCC 16.2.1 and Clang 22.1.8 on the machine but does not say which compiler built the published runs.
hardware: Intel Core i7-10510U (Comet Lake) laptop, AVX2+BMI1+BMI2+ERMS+FMA, glibc 2.44, Linux 7.2
tradeoffs: Drop-in asm_* API rather than libc symbols; x86-64 needs AVX2/BMI2; AArch64 port uses NEON; math is freestanding C.
caveats: Numbers are noisy laptop best-of-N results (author says so); the memory/string results are published only as approximate ranges and glibc wins on strlen and strstr. The memchr workload in bench/bench.c searches a repeating a-z string for 'z', so every size of 26 bytes or more measures a hit at offset 25, and the '1.1-1.2x from 128 B up' figure is really a 26-byte scan; memcmp compares a buffer with itself (equal-input case only). The 'memmem several times faster' claim has no benchmark. The snprintf table (docs/BENCHMARKS.md last changed 2026-09-28) was measured on the minimal hand-written asm_snprintf, which CHANGELOG [Unreleased] says was removed on 2026-10-06 in favour of the portable C printf engine (src/libc/printf.c); the current asm_snprintf is unmeasured C. asm_u64toa is a dedicated converter timed against general snprintf("%llu"). The arena and malloc-heap wins come from a different allocation model (bump arena with O(1) reset, thread-local cache), not from assembly alone. The libm routines are portable C adapted from musl (MIT), not assembly, so the cbrt/cosh/asinh wins are not asm-kernel results. Single machine; which of GCC 16.2.1 or Clang 22.1.8 built the harness is unstated. Young repo with 0 stars.

claimed_speedup: 32 B (16,777,216 copies, both aligned) memcpy_fast 81 ms vs memcpy 281 ms (3.5x, derived); 64 B 91 vs 364 ms (4.0x, derived); 512 B 124 vs 242 ms; 8 KiB 55 vs 70 ms; 8 MiB 287 vs 421 ms (1.5x, derived); random access 487 vs 1000 ms. compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.9: gcc -O3 -msse2 FastMemcpy.c (AVX: -O3 -mavx FastMemcpy_Avx.c); msvc 2012: cl -arch:SSE2 -O2
tradeoffs: SSE2 or AVX only; jump table for small sizes, non-temporal stores and prefetch for huge sizes.
caveats: Implementation is SSE2/AVX intrinsics (85 _mm_ calls in FastMemcpy.h, 91 in FastMemcpy_Avx.h, no inline asm), so it is a memcpy-baseline entry rather than hand-written assembly. CPU model and glibc version not stated; the README results are from 2015 (gcc 4.9 / MSVC 2012); the 2017 AVX version has no published numbers. Only one README row is slower (1 MiB, both aligned: 181 vs 165 ms); the others show gains. Harness flaws (FastMemcpy.c): same src/dst and size every call (hot cache, perfectly predicted branches), millisecond gettimeofday timer, memcpy always runs first on freshly malloc'd buffers, benchmark() not marked noinline so sizes may be constant-propagated; alexey-milovidov (issue #6) called the benchmark 'nonsense' for these reasons and saw glibc slightly faster in a ClickHouse perf test. Independent runs on newer toolchains show it slower than glibc memcpy: issue #4 (gcc 7.5.0, glibc 2.27: 32 B 230 vs 63 ms, random 1953 vs 635 ms; gcc 5.4: 512 B 77 vs 56 ms) and issue #6 (gcc 10.2.1, Clear Linux: 32 B 48 vs 35 ms, 1024 B 85 vs 41 ms, random 802 vs 662 ms). Issue #5 (gcc 4.4.7, 278 vs 85 ms at 32 B) was a build-flag mistake per the reporter.

The shipped test/bench.sh actually generates and times a 500 MB file and has no fmt row, so the published 1 GB table is not what the script as written produces.

SIMD microbenchmark, ASM vs naive C at gcc -O2: scan_count_byte 8.9 vs 3.3 GB/s (2.7x), scan_find_byte 11.3 vs 2.3 GB/s (5.0x), scan_find_byte early hit 8 ns vs 88 ns (10.8x), parse_get_field ~20 ns vs ~50 ns (~2.5x).
compiler_and_flags: Release build per Makefile: NASM -f elf64 -O2 for the assembly, gcc -O2 -DNDEBUG for the C argument parser; microbenchmark C reference built with gcc -O2 (BENCHMARKS.md, test/bench.c); gcc version and xsv build not stated
hardware: WSL2, Intel Core (model not stated), DDR4-3200
tradeoffs: Linux x86-64 only (AVX2 plus CPUID dispatch), mmap-based; join, sample, split, flatten and table are not implemented.
caveats: No CPU model (only 'Intel Core' under WSL2), no gcc version, no xsv version or build, no run-to-run spread. The xsv baseline ran far below xsv's own published throughput: 1 GiB in 13.14 s for count is about 82 MB/s and index about 75 MB/s, versus 413.76 MB/s and 379.28 MB/s in xsv's BENCHMARKS.md on an i7-6900K (derived from page data), which points at a slow WSL2 file path or build rather than parsing cost, so the 5.7-76x ratios are likely inflated. oxsv does less work by default: count only counts newline bytes, and quoted-field parsing is off unless --quote is given, whereas xsv always runs a full RFC 4180 parser; the generated test data has no quoted fields, so outputs agree here but would differ on CSV with quoted commas or newlines. search is exact match versus xsv's regex. oxsv memory-maps the file (an I/O strategy difference). name: CAFS (cache-aware frequency sort)
baseline: vqsort (Google Highway), std::sort, pdqsort, IPS4o, ska_sort
workload: Sorting integer arrays with N elements and K distinct values over a 1600-point (N, K) grid, 592,770 measurements, AVX2 hot loop (one cmpeq per element on 64-byte buckets).
claimed_speedup: Bin-mean speedup 1.7-3.1x vs pdqsort, 1.97-3.52x vs IPS4o, 1.27-2.34x vs vqsort, 4-17x vs ska_sort and 8-17x vs std::sort across the K << N band (README table, K = 4 to 8 distinct values: std::sort 17.10x, ska_sort 16.96x, IPS4o 3.50x, pdqsort 3.10x, vqsort 1.32x). It loses where K approaches N: bin-mean 0.60 vs vqsort and 0.66 vs ska_sort for K of 8.4e6 to 1.7e7, and the README says vqsort wins by 1.5 to 2 times beyond K = 6.7e5.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 13.2 -O3 -mavx2 -mbmi -DNDEBUG (Windows 11); benchmark/main_bigdata.cpp in the repo
hardware: Intel Core i5-12400F, 32 GB DDR4-3200
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, x86-64 with AVX2 and BMI only; targets integer columns with few distinct values; an adaptive dispatcher falls back to pdqsort for high-entropy input (worst case observed about 5x pdqsort time). Primarily a sorting algorithm that uses SIMD, so it may belong with the sorting lists.
caveats: Very new single-author repo (7 commits, 2026-05-09 to 2026-08-07, 32 stars); all numbers from one Windows 11 desktop (i5-12400F, AVX2 path only, no AVX-512 run of vqsort). std::sort is libstdc++ (inferred from the g++ 13.2 toolchain; the README does not name the library). Timings are best of 2 runs per (N, K) point with high_resolution_clock, on uint64 keys drawn from a K-value palette spread over the 64-bit range; only the u64 path is benchmarked although int32/int64 specializations exist. The raw CSV is not in the repo (README says it ships with the preprint artifact); arXiv 2605.25040 exists (seen via a search snippet only, arXiv blocked) and is not peer reviewed. The README is internally inconsistent about std::sort: its crossover line says std::sort reaches parity at K = 1.7e7, while the table shows 3.47x for that bin and the operational table says CAFS still wins at K = N. CAFS loses to vqsort (0.60x) and ska_sort (0.66x) near K = N, and the dispatcher's worst case is about 5x pdqsort time. name: marcelcases/simd (std::experimental::simd kernels)
baseline: scalar C++ version of each kernel built with compiler auto-vectorization disabled (-fno-tree-vectorize)
workload: Seven exercises (nine kernel rows: element-wise add, memory-bound FMA, sum reduction, dot product, upper-bound clamp, count above threshold, stable softmax, horizontal blur, 1D convolution) written with libstdc++ std::experimental::simd versus scalar versions; 16,777,216 floats for the first four, 4,194,304 for softmax, a 1920x1080 grayscale image for blur, 1,048,576 floats for convolution; median of 9 samples.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+, one pinned core, GCC 14.1: sum reduction 5.37x, 1D convolution 5.89x, upper-bound clamp 6.81x, count above threshold 4.85x, horizontal blur 2.12x, dot product 1.78x, element-wise add 1.62x, softmax 1.57x, memory-bound FMA 1.04x. icpx 2025.2 on the same CPU: clamp 10.29x, dot product 4.45x, sum reduction 5.32x. Apple M1 Pro, GCC 15.2.0: count above threshold 24.51x, clamp 20.00x, sum reduction 4.00x, 1D convolution 4.02x, element-wise add 2.60x. Banana Pi F3 (RVV 1.0, VL=8): sum reduction 4.51x, 1D convolution 2.15x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.1 (MareNostrum 5), icpx 2025.2, Homebrew GCC 15.2.0 (M1), conda-forge GCC 16.2 cross-compiler (RISC-V). Makefile: Linux -std=c++2b -O3 -march=native -mavx512f -mavx512vl -mavx512dq -mavx512bw -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math; macOS arm64 -std=c++2b -O3 -mcpu=apple-m1 -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math; RISC-V (README) -std=c++23 -O3 -march=rv64gcv_zvl256b -mrvv-vector-bits=zvl -static -fno-math-errno -fno-trapping-math. Scalar builds add -fno-tree-vectorize -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns (GCC) or -fno-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize (icpx/clang). RISC-V VL=4 and VL=8 variants used separate builds with temporary SIMD aliases not in the repo.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ (MareNostrum 5 GPP, one pinned core, exclusive node); Banana Pi F3 (RISC-V RVV 1.0, 256-bit VLEN); Apple M1 Pro (4-lane NEON, not pinned)
tradeoffs: Needs a C++23 compiler with libstdc++ <experimental/simd> (GCC); does not use C++26 <simd>. Makefile defaults target MareNostrum 5 AVX-512 and Apple M1, not generic hosts. Portable across x86-64, AArch64 and RISC-V RVV, but the RISC-V toolchain reports one lane for native_simd<float>, so fixed widths 4 and 8 were used.
caveats: Teaching study, not a reusable library; the SIMD side is libstdc++'s std::experimental::simd itself (std::simd is one of the category's listed baselines), so the entry measures std::simd code against scalar loops, not a library beating an incumbent. The baseline is deliberately de-vectorized scalar code, so the speedups say little about beating a normally compiled -O3 build; the exception is sum reduction and dot product, which GCC cannot auto-vectorize at -O3 without -ffast-math anyway, so those rows (5.37x and 1.78x on the Xeon with GCC) are the ones that would hold against a plain -O3 build. Element-wise add and memory-bound FMA are memory-traffic-limited (1.01x to 1.65x on x86 and RISC-V). The README itself notes that count_above on RISC-V contained no RVV instructions (gain is scalar unrolling), that icpx vectorizes softmax's exp loop through SVML, and that the large M1 clamp/count gains come from replacing branches with masks. x86 exercises 1-5 used three initial warm-ups instead of per-sample warm-ups and have not been refreshed. The RISC-V VL=4/VL=8 variants cannot be rebuilt from the repo (temporary aliases), and no result CSVs are committed (results/ is absent). M1 run had no core pinning. Repository history starts 2026-09-03, 0 stars, so results are unreviewed.

name: positional-popcount
baseline: pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive (portable scalar C, auto-vectorized by GCC) and pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive_nosimd
workload: Positional population count (set-bit counts at each of 16 bit positions) over arrays of 16-bit values; the speedup tables cover arrays of 128 to 65536 values on one core, while the cycles-per-integer and MB/s tables use 1 million uniformly random simulated FLAG fields over 1,000 repetitions.
claimed_speedup: pospopcnt_u16_avx512_harley_seal is 16.28x faster than the auto-vectorized scalar naive version at 65536 values (6.43x at 4096, 9.41x at 8192) and 138.71x faster than the no-SIMD naive version at 65536 values; AVX-512 adder forest 4.96x at 2048; at 128 values the Harley-Seal version is 0.52x (slower). README also states about 50 GB/s (about 0.120 cycles per 16-bit integer) with AVX-512.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 7.3.1 20180303 (Red Hat 7.3.1-5); Makefile OPTFLAGS -O3 -march=native, CFLAGS -std=c99, bench built with -std=c++11
hardware: Cannon Lake Core i3-8121U for the speedup table; cycles and MB/s tables also give Sky Lake Xeon W-2104 and Haswell Xeon E5-2697 v3
stars_or_usage: 57 stars; code of the paper 'Efficient Computation of Positional Population Counts Using SIMD Instructions' (Klarqvist, Muła, Lemire), Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience 33(17), 2021, DOI 10.1002/cpe.6304 (venue from search snippet; arXiv 1911.02696); README points production users to libalgebra
tradeoffs: Fastest variants need AVX-512 (Cannon Lake / Skylake-X class); SSE and AVX2 fallbacks are included; experimental repo, the README points production users to libalgebra.h; small arrays (under about 512 values) can be slower than the scalar path.
caveats: Speedup-table baseline is the compiler auto-vectorized scalar version at -O3 -march=native, a fair baseline; the 138.71x figure is against a deliberately non-vectorized baseline. Speedup table comes from one 2019-era laptop-class Cannon Lake CPU; the AVX-512 paths do not run on most AMD or client Intel parts of that era. The README tables predate the final code: the cycles and MB/s tables list methods (pospopcnt_u16_avx512_csa, avx2_csa, mula3) that no longer exist under those names in pospopcnt.c, and the speedup table's avx512_adder_forest/blend names are now avx512bw_*. Timing uses CPUID/RDTSC serialization per call and the input is regenerated and pre-touched by the reference function before each timed call, so small-array (128-512 values) ratios include fixed overhead and warm-cache effects. Peer-reviewed in CCPE 2021 (venue from search snippet only; arXiv not reachable). libalgebra (same author) reuses these kernels, so the two entries overlap; a follow-up paper (arXiv 2412.16370, Clausecker, Lemire, Schintke) extends the method to AVX2, AVX-512 and ASIMD.

name: Pure SIMD (pure_simd)
baseline: scalar_shader, the same per-pixel shader written as a plain scalar C++ loop in the repo's benchmark directory
workload: Per-pixel integer shader over a 512x512 int screen buffer (99 iterations of multiply and modulo-by-constant integer arithmetic per pixel), pure_simd_shader instantiated with vector sizes 1 to 128, against the same loop written in plain scalar C++.
claimed_speedup: Scalar 103 ms vs pure_simd width 64 10.9 ms (about 9.4x, derived from page data); width 32 12.5 ms, width 16 16.2 ms, width 8 28.0 ms; width 128 regresses to 158 ms (slower than scalar).
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 9.0 -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel Core i7-9750H, Ubuntu 18.04
tradeoffs: No intrinsics: variadic-template unrolled vector types that rely on the compiler's SLP vectorizer (gcc or clang needed). Vector width must be tuned (too wide hurts the instruction cache). Header-only C++17; Conan is needed to build the tests and benchmarks.
caveats: A single toy workload (one shader adapted from the 'Practical SIMD Programming' tutorial) on one laptop CPU; the scalar baseline is the author's own loop with the same flags. Its inner loop is a serial 99-step dependency chain per pixel, so the gain comes from the compiler SLP-vectorizing the unrolled independent pixels, while the scalar loop as written evidently was not vectorized (it ties vector size 1 at 103 ms) and size 128 is 1.5x slower (158 ms). The shader relies on signed 32-bit overflow (px*py terms exceed INT_MAX), which is undefined behaviour in both versions; outputs match in the repo's test. The second benchmark (benchmark/sum.cpp) has no published results. Numbers are aggregate means of 10 repetitions. No comparison with Highway, xsimd, Eigen or std::simd; the README calls the library experimental with unstable interfaces.

claimed_speedup: i3-6100, g++ -m64 -Ofast -march=native, 1-byte elements, bswap variant vs std::reverse: 1000 elements 290 ns vs 36 ns (8.056x); 10000: 2740 vs 191 ns (14.346x); 100000: 27511 vs 1739 ns (15.820x); 1,000,000: 279525 vs 24710 ns (11.312x); 8 elements 19 vs 19 ns (1.000x). SSSE3 variant peaks at 10.510x (10000 elements) and the AVX2 variant at 16.053x (100000 elements: 27515 vs 1714 ns). AVX512 on i9-7900x, built with Visual Studio 2017 x64-Release: peak 22.357x at 10000 elements (2504 vs 112 ns), 11.153x at 1,000,000. The top-of-README speedup table (AVX2 x22.032 and AVX512 x22.357 on i9-7900x, AVX2 x16.053 on i3-6100) lists peak speedups over std::reverse (the 'Serial' x1 column); the i3-6100 and i9-7900x AVX512 values equal the peaks of the std::reverse tables (derived from page data), while the i5-8600K, E5-2697 v4 and BCM2837 rows have no table or flags behind them.
compiler_and_flags: i3-6100 run: g++ -m64 -Ofast -march=native; i9-7900X AVX-512 run: Visual Studio 2017 x64 Release
hardware: Intel Core i3-6100 (8 GB DDR4), Core i9-7900X, Core i5-8600K, Xeon E5-2697 v4, Broadcom BCM2837 (Raspberry Pi)

name: sse-popcount
baseline: scalar hardware POPCNT instruction loop (cpu / builtin-popcnt via __builtin_popcountll), plus lookup-table and bit-parallel scalar versions
workload: Population count over 32 B to 4096 B buffers, repeated a fixed number of times (5 runs), times reported in seconds per procedure; AVX2/AVX-512 Harley-Seal and PSHUFB-lookup versus scalar POPCNT.
claimed_speedup: Cascade Lake Xeon Gold 6240, gcc 8.3.0, 4096 B: avx512-harley-seal 0.04826 s versus cpu (64-bit POPCNT loop) 0.17391 s and builtin-popcnt 0.25037 s, about 3.6x and 5.2x; avx2-harley-seal 0.09748 s versus cpu 0.17391 s, about 1.8x; against the fastest scalar row (builtin-popcnt-unrolled-errata 0.16751 s) about 3.5x for AVX-512 and 1.7x for AVX2 (all derived from page data). The POPCNT loop wins up to 512 B: avx512-harley-seal 2.99407 s versus cpu 0.30912 s at 32 B and 0.25122 s versus 0.16864 s at 512 B; the AVX-512 version first wins at 1024 B (0.09325 s versus 0.19950 s). Haswell i7-4770, gcc 5.3.0: avx2-harley-seal 0.11145 s versus cpu 0.19857 s at 4096 B, about 1.8x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.3.0 (crosstool-NG 1.24.0) for the Cascade Lake run (2021-02-24). Flags are not printed in the result file; the Makefile in force at that date (commit ba36276, 2019-12-08; next Makefile change 2023-08-20) sets -std=c++11 -O2 -Wall -pedantic -Wextra -Wfatal-errors -mpopcnt -fabi-version=6 plus -mavx512bw -DHAVE_AVX512BW_INSTRUCTIONS for the AVX512BW target (the current Makefile uses -std=c++17).
hardware: Cascade Lake Xeon Gold 6240 @ 2.6 GHz (AVX512BW), generated 2021-02-24; the repo also has Haswell i7-4770, Skylake i7-6700, Skylake-X, Cannon Lake i3-8121U, Sandy Bridge-E, Westmere, Bulldozer and ARM result files
stars_or_usage: 357 stars; companion repo of the Muła, Kurz and Lemire paper 'Faster Population Counts Using AVX2 Instructions' (arXiv 1611.07612, Computer Journal 2018)
tradeoffs: x86-specific sample programs (SSSE3/AVX2/AVX-512BW/VBMI), not a packaged library; needs a CPU with the matching extension and loses to the POPCNT instruction below roughly 512 B; kimwalisch/libpopcnt is the packaged, runtime-dispatched version of the same ideas.

This repo is sample/benchmark code for the Mula, Kurz and Lemire paper 'Faster Population Counts Using AVX2 Instructions' (arXiv 1611.07612, Computer Journal 2018; paper not opened, arXiv blocked); the packaged library form is kimwalisch/libpopcnt (already listed in wave 11).
