name: ultraviolet
baseline: glam single-lane types (glam_f32x1) in mathbench; nalgebra wide types tie
workload: mathbench-rs 'wide' benchmarks processing batches of 16 to 80000 elements with structure-of-arrays f32x4 and f32x8 types: euler rotations, ray-sphere intersection, matrix4 determinant/inverse/multiply, vector3 cross/dot/normalize.
claimed_speedup: mathbench wide table, Ryzen 7 3800X, RUSTFLAGS -C target-feature=+avx2: ultraviolet_f32x8 vs glam_f32x1: euler 2d x80000 18.94 us vs 41.87 us (about 2.2x), euler 3d x80000 28.54 us vs 58.97 us (about 2.1x), ray-sphere intersection x80000 25.26 us vs 497.6 us (about 20x), matrix4 determinant x16 14.6545 ns vs 62.0342 ns (about 4.2x), vector3 normalize x16 7.3365 ns vs 35.2002 ns (about 4.8x), all ratios derived from page data. nalgebra_f32x8 is equal or within noise (euler 2d 18.57 us). Not faster everywhere: glam_f32x1 wins matrix4 transpose x16 (73.5089 ns vs 96.3356 ns for ultraviolet_f32x8) and ties matrix4 mul matrix4 x16 (163.5378 ns vs 167.0614 ns); at x256 most rows are ties (matrix2 mul matrix2 x256 688.9 ns vs 678.7 ns, transform point2 x256 691.8 ns vs 683.6 ns).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28), RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+avx2' cargo bench --features wide wide; ultraviolet 0.10.0; tables produced at mathbench-rs commit 8e5467c (2026-10-10)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, Linux
tradeoffs: Requires an SoA/AoSoA data layout (wide f32x4 and f32x8 types) rather than ordinary Vec3 structs; AVX2 must be enabled explicitly at build time. Rust only.
caveats: The comparison is against glam's one-lane scalar type doing the same amount of work, so the large ratios mostly measure SoA batching, not a better library; nalgebra's f32x8 types match ultraviolet, and glam_f32x1 still wins matrix4 transpose x16 and ties matrix4 mul matrix4 x16, while ultraviolet_f32x4 is slower than glam on matrix2 and matrix3 transpose x16. Gains shrink to ties at x256 sizes. In mathbench's scalar table ultraviolet wins outright only the matrix2 and matrix3 transpose rows. The ray-sphere ratio (about 20x for 4-8 lanes) suggests the glam_f32x1 path is unusually slow on that row: 497.6 us for x80000 is about 4.7x glam's own scalar-table rate of 13.37 us per x10000 (derived from page data). mathbench is written by glam's author. The tables predate mathbench 0.5.0 (2026-10-11 rewrite to batched per-element throughput at sizes 16 and 1024; wide 'return self' rows were deleted by hand), so HEAD does not reproduce the exact rows. The repository has moved to github.com/fu5ha/ultraviolet (Cargo.toml and crates.io still name termhn). No license text file exists in the repo (LICENSE, LICENSE-MIT, LICENSE-APACHE, LICENSE-ZLIB all 404); the MIT OR Apache-2.0 OR Zlib expression is only in Cargo.toml and crates.io metadata. name: ARM NEON Compositor
baseline: the same alpha-overlay routine without NEON intrinsics, compiled with GCC -O3
workload: overlay_alpha_stride (div255_round) on random square BGRA images, sides 1-200 px in steps of 1 (small) and 50-5000 px in 100 steps (large), called through Python ctypes by examples/perf_test/perf_test.py. Time per call is averaged over max_size*10/size iterations, one run per size. The NEON build is compared with the same library built with DISABLE_NEON (scalar fallback with GCC unroll/ivdep pragmas, left to GCC -O3 auto-vectorization).
claimed_speedup: README text: up to 3.5x faster than the same routine without NEON intrinsics for small images, and around 1.4x for very large images. From the committed CSVs (examples/perf_test/output, derived from page data): for square images of 1-200 px per side, 0.93x at 1 px (NEON slower), 1.40x at 33 px, 2.53x at 97 px and 3.47x at 200 px, with a maximum of 3.58x at 186 px; for 50-5000 px, 1.37-1.40x from 450 to 1650 px, rising to 1.54-1.59x from 2450 to 5000 px.
compiler_and_flags: GCC -O3 (version not stated)
hardware: Raspberry Pi 3B+, Ubuntu 20.04 64-bit
tradeoffs: ARM NEON only (AArch64 Raspberry Pi class); GPL-3.0 licence. Narrow function (alpha overlay), not a general SIMD library.
caveats: The baseline is the library's own non-NEON fallback (overlay_alpha_1 looped 8x under '#pragma GCC unroll 8' and 'ivdep'), not an external incumbent such as OpenCV. GCC version unstated, and the gain depends on how well that version auto-vectorizes the fallback. Timing runs from Python via ctypes, and both paths use '#pragma omp parallel for', so a fixed per-call overhead of about 20 us deflates the ratios below about 30 px (NEON is 0.93x at 1 px). It is not documented whether the committed .so files were built with OpenMP. Each size was run once with no variance reported. Raw data is public in examples/perf_test/output, and the prebuilt aarch64 and x86_64 .so files are committed.

Unequal kernels: the SIMD map and reduce benchmarks call faster's rsqrt, which on x86 is the approximate _mm256_rsqrt_ps/_mm_rsqrt_ps (the trait documents significant error past 1e-3), while the scalar baseline does an exact sqrt().recip(), i.e. one extra sqrt and a division per element; the ceil() in the chain hides the approximation for the constant input -123.456, so results match, but part of the 7.9x comes from cheaper math rather than SIMD width alone. The input is a constant-filled 1024-element array. Some SIMD rows are slower than scalar (zip_simd on AVX, determinant3 and nop on the pentium polyfill target). The crate never built on stable Rust: it needs nightly with #![feature(stdsimd)] and packed_simd_2; the stdsimd feature gate was later removed from nightly, so it likely does not build on current toolchains (not built here). name: ISPC (Intel SPMD Program Compiler)
baseline: reference serial C++ implementations of the examples/ workloads (gcc 4.2.1 on OS X 10.7.2; MSVC 2010 on Windows Server 2008 for the 40-core table)
workload: The example programs in the repo's examples/ directory (aobench, binomial and Black-Scholes options pricing, Mandelbrot, ray tracer, 3D stencil, volume rendering; perf page adds deferred shading and Perlin noise), each timed against its included serial C++ reference (minimum of several runs; the examples print '(N.NNx speedup from ISPC)').
claimed_speedup: InPar 2012 paper Table 2 (4-core 3.4 GHz Core i7 iMac, 8-wide AVX), versus serial non-SIMD C++: 1 core / 1 thread aobench 5.58x, Binomial Options 4.39x, Black-Scholes 7.43x, Mandelbrot 5.85x, Ray Tracer 6.85x, Stencil 3.37x, Volume Rendering 3.24x (geomean about 5.0x, derived from page data); 4 cores / 8 threads 12.03x-34.82x. Table 3 (40-core Xeon E7-8870, SSE4, 80 threads, MSVC 2010 serial baseline): 9.40x-243.18x. SSE to AVX geomean 1.42x. README: 'frequently provides a 3x or more speedup on architectures with 4-wide vector SSE units and 5x-6x on architectures with 8-wide AVX vector units'. ispc.github.io/perf.html (gcc 4.2.1 serial baseline on the same iMac): 1 core 3.60x-8.45x, 4 cores 15.53x-33.43x.
compiler_and_flags: ispc of 2011-2012 (built on LLVM); serial C++ baseline compiled with clang built from the same LLVM (paper notes gcc gave essentially the same results); 40-core runs used MSVC 2010; perf page used gcc 4.2.1 (OS X 10.7.2). Optimization flags not stated.
hardware: 4-core 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7 Apple iMac with AVX (exact model not stated; first-generation AVX, Sandy Bridge era) for Table 2 and the perf page; 2-way hyper-threaded 40-core Intel Xeon E7-8870 at 2.40 GHz with SSE4 on Windows Server 2008 for Table 3.
tradeoffs: A separate SPMD language and compiler (outputs object files callable from C/C++) rather than an intrinsics library; targets x86 SSE2/SSE4/AVX/AVX2/AVX-512, ARM NEON and Intel GPUs. Examples are in the repo's examples/ directory.
caveats: Evidence is from ISPC's Intel authors: a peer-reviewed paper (InPar 2012) plus Intel's perf page, both measured around 2011-2012 on first-generation AVX and SSE4 hardware with an unnamed Core i7 model, unstated flags and an unstated ispc version; nothing newer is published. The baseline is serial non-SIMD C++ (both versions 'received equivalent amounts of performance tuning'), not hand-written intrinsics or SIMD libraries (Highway, xsimd); the paper gives only user anecdotes for intrinsics parity (0.99x-1.05x). Multi-core figures combine task parallelism and hyper-threading with SIMD. ispc is a compiler for an SPMD C dialect, not an intrinsics library, so the category fit is loose. The ispc.github.io perf page was read from its source in the ispc/ispc.github.com repo (github.io blocked here).

name: libalgebra
baseline: naive scalar code with auto-vectorization disabled (__attribute__((optimize("no-tree-vectorize")))): popcount_scalar_naive_nosimd and intersect/union/diff_scalar_naive_nosimd, which count bits with an 8-bit lookup table (STORM_popcnt_lookup8bit), not the POPCNT instruction
workload: Popcount, positional popcount and bitmap set-algebra cardinalities (AND/OR/XOR) over arrays of 4 to 1048576 64-bit words, in CPU cycles per word on an AVX512BW machine.
claimed_speedup: Popcount: 16.4x at 1024 64-bit words, 21x at 8192, 4.2x at 1048576 (1.0x at 4 words); set-algebra cardinality (AND/OR/XOR): 15.3x at 1024 word pairs, 13.7x at 8192, 2.8x at 1048576, 0.8x at 4; all in CPU cycles per 64-bit word versus an 8-bit lookup-table scalar loop compiled with vectorization disabled. The README also shows a positional-popcount table (up to 138.71x at 65536 values for pospopcnt_u16_avx512_harvey_seal), but those numbers are identical to the mklarqvist/positional-popcount README (measured there with gcc 7.3.1) and are not produced by libalgebra's benchmark.cpp.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 8.2.1 20180905 (Red Hat 8.2.1-3) per README; CMakeLists.txt forces CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release and sets CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS to -std=c++11 (CMake's GCC Release default adds -O3 -DNDEBUG); no -march flag, the SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX512BW kernels use __attribute__((target(...))) with CPUID dispatch; run as 'benchmark -p -r 10000'
hardware: Cannon Lake Core i3-8121U (AVX512BW)
tradeoffs: Header-only C/C++ library using POPCNT, SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX512BW and NEON; tested with GCC, Clang and MSVC per the README.
caveats: Baseline is a deliberately naive 8-bit lookup-table loop with vectorization disabled (about 8.1 cycles per 64-bit word for popcount, 5.0 for set algebra), not the POPCNT instruction or __builtin_popcountll, so the speedups overstate the gain over a tuned scalar loop. The positional-popcount table in the README is copied from mklarqvist/positional-popcount (same numbers, measured there with gcc 7.3.1); libalgebra's benchmark.cpp does not benchmark pospopcnt. The library packages kernels from positional-popcount and the Lemire/Kurz/Mula AVX2 popcount work (sse-popcount), so it overlaps with those entries. Release build defines NDEBUG, so the assert(a == b) correctness check in the perf popcount path is compiled out and the set-algebra path has no check. Single machine; data freshly generated each iteration and cache-resident (README calls it a practical upper limit). No commits since 2019-12-16.

name: math_intrinsics
baseline: C standard library scalar float math functions (acosf, asinf, atanf, cbrtf, cosf, sinf, expf, exp2f, logf, log2f); libc and compiler not stated
workload: tests/benchmark.c (README run matches commit a9e8fe5, NUM_ITERATIONS 1,000,000,000; current code uses 200,000,000): the AVX2 loop evaluates 8 independent lanes starting at 0..0.875 and stepping by FLT_EPSILON (inputs stay in about [0, 2]); the C std loop calls acosf/asinf/atanf/cbrtf/cosf/sinf/expf/exp2f/logf/log2f through a function pointer in a serial dependency chain total += f(total), seeded with the SIMD time in ms.
claimed_speedup: AVX2 vs C std: acos 723.7 ms vs 5408.2 ms (7.47x), asin 7.83x, atan 5.13x, cbrt 12.84x, cos 17.62x, sin 18.14x, exp 5.30x, exp2 2.06x, log 16.51x, log2 7.50x. The __MATH_INTRINSINCS_FAST__ mode adds roughly 1.4x to 1.9x for sin, cos, acos, asin, exp2 and pow.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -mavx2 -mfma for the benchmark targets (tests/CMakeLists.txt, non-MSVC); compiler of the README run not stated (CI builds with clang on ubuntu-latest and the default compiler on macos-latest)
hardware: old Intel Core i7 from 2018 (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Single header; AVX2 (x86) and NEON (checked manually on an M1 Pro, not in CI); float only; max errors around 1e-7 for most functions, up to 6.5e-5 for acos/asin in fast mode. Author states performance is not the focus.
caveats: Baseline harness is not like-for-like: the SIMD side is a throughput loop over 8 independent lanes with inputs in about [0, 2], while the libm side is a latency-bound serial chain total += f(total) seeded with the SIMD time in milliseconds (README run, commit a9e8fe5), so acosf/asinf received |x|>1 and then NaN for the whole run, expf/exp2f overflowed to +inf after the first call and sinf/cosf ran on arguments near 880 (current code seeds with seconds, but log2f still drops to NaN and acosf/asinf still leave the domain after one or two calls). The 2.06x-18.14x ratios are therefore not a valid measure of speed against libm. Compiler, libm (glibc or Apple) and CPU model of the README run are not stated ('old Intel Core i7 from 2018'). The author writes 'Performance is not the focus.' The benchmark source is tests/benchmark.c (not visible in the repo root). Fast-mode gains (~1.4x-1.9x for sin, cos, acos, asin, exp2, pow) are against the library's own precise mode. No comparison with SLEEF or xsimd math (both catalogued).

name: ParallelReductionsBenchmark
baseline: std::accumulate (serial)
workload: Summing a 1 GB array (268,435,456 floats, all set to 1.0f by std::fill_n) with serial std::accumulate, an 8-accumulator unrolled loop, hand-written SSE/AVX2/AVX-512, NEON and SVE kernels, OpenMP, fork_union, Taskflow, std::reduce with execution policies, Thrust, CUB and CUDA kernels, reported in bytes/s with an error% column against the exact sum n.
claimed_speedup: Single thread versus serial std::accumulate (libstdc++, GCC 12), 1 GB array of 1.0f, README tables. AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl: unrolled/f64 14.7387 GB/s vs std::accumulate/f64 5.58465 GB/s (about 2.6x, derived from page data, both exact); unrolled/f32 28.2311 GB/s, neon/f32 22.2544 GB/s and sve/f32 21.4542 GB/s vs std::accumulate/f32 5.58767 GB/s (about 5.1x, 4.0x and 3.8x, derived from page data). AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl: unrolled<f64> 34.0189 GB/s and avx2<f64> 19.3258 GB/s vs std::accumulate<f64> 4.88389 GB/s (about 7.0x and 4.0x, derived from page data, exact); unrolled<f32> 35.1514, avx2<f32> 33.3195 and avx512<f32interleaving> 26.8351 GB/s vs std::accumulate<f32> 4.88655 GB/s (about 7.2x, 6.8x and 5.5x, derived from page data); avx2<f32kahan> 9.73619 GB/s, exact, about 2.0x std::accumulate (derived from page data). Nvidia DGX-H100 host: avx2<f32> 9.69112 vs std::accumulate<f32> 5.5322 GB/s (about 1.75x, derived from page data). Multithreaded std::reduce<par> (368.528 GB/s on Zen4, 550.384 GB/s on Graviton4) is libstdc++'s own parallel algorithm on oneTBB, not this repository's code.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12 (NVCC 12.1 for the CUDA rows); CMakeLists.txt defaults to Release and appends -O2 to CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE (effective -O2) and sets -march=native -fopenmp for GCC; the Apple M2 Pro table names no compiler
hardware: AWS Graviton4 (c8g.metal-24xl, 96 cores), AWS m7a.metal-48xl (AMD Zen4, 192 threads at 3701.95 MHz; CPU model string not printed), Nvidia DGX-H100 node (160 threads at 2100 MHz; CPU model not named), Apple M2 Pro
tradeoffs: Educational benchmark harness rather than a drop-in library. Hand-written AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels are x86 only; NEON and SVE variants exist for Arm. Huge pages, NUMA and Kahan summation are handled by hand.
caveats: This is an educational benchmark collection, not a reusable library, and it has no LICENSE file (raw LICENSE returns 404, no licence in the GitHub sidebar or Cargo.toml), so it is reference only. The baseline is std::accumulate, whose required left-to-right fold is latency-bound on the float add chain at -O2 without -ffast-math; most of the gain comes from reassociation with multiple accumulators, and no single-threaded std::reduce (or unseq) row is measured, which is the standard library's own reassociating alternative. Hand-written intrinsics do not beat the plain unrolled C++ loop in most tables: on Zen4 avx2<f32> 33.32, avx2<f64> 19.33 and avx512<f32interleaving> 26.84 GB/s are all below unrolled<f32> 35.15 / unrolled<f64> 34.02 GB/s, and on Graviton4 neon/f32 22.25 and sve/f32 21.45 GB/s are below unrolled/f32 28.23 GB/s, contradicting the README's statement that hand-written AVX2 beats auto-vectorization (it holds only on the DGX-H100 host). All f32 rows give wrong sums because the input is 2^28 ones and each f32 accumulator saturates at 2^24 (std::accumulate<f32> 93.75% error, unrolled<f32> 50%, neon/sve 75%); only f64 and Kahan rows are exact, and avx2<f32kahan> is about 2x std::accumulate on Zen4. The DGX-H100 table's std::reduce<par, f64> and <par_unseq, f64> rows report 100% error. The Zen4 and DGX tables use older row labels and predate the 2025 code. Single hand-pasted runs with no variance. The README's own conclusion is that multithreaded std::reduce is the CPU winner.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/topics/sve (C++ list) surfaced the repo; README result tables for DGX-H100 and AWS Zen4 read directly

name: qHilbert
baseline: Wikipedia d2xy/rot C implementation (in source/qHilbert.cpp), called once per index from tests/benchmark.cpp; the README table does not label it
workload: tests/benchmark.cpp: map all 16,384 indices of an order-7 (128x128) Hilbert curve to 2D points, 10 trials averaged with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock, output checked against d2xy (PASS/FAIL). qHilbert2D uses the Hacker's Delight (Lam-Shapiro/Steele) parallel-prefix method, with pext under BMI2 and SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512 paths.
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt: -Ofast -Wall -Wextra on the GCC branch, plus -mbmi2 / -msse4.2 / -mavx2 / -mavx512f per Benchmark-* executable; compiler and version not stated
tradeoffs: x86 SIMD (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512 plus BMI2 pext); a NEON version is shown in the README as illustration. Uses glm::u32vec2 for output points.
caveats: The table's baseline (Wikipedia d2xy, branchy loop with one cross-translation-unit call per point and no LTO) is not labelled on the README; it is identified from tests/benchmark.cpp. Most of the gain is algorithmic (Hacker's Delight parallel-prefix rewrite): the Serial/BMI2 column is already x42.5 on i9-7900x, AVX-512 adds about 1.19x over it (derived from page data), and AVX2 is slower than SSE4.2 on E5-2697 v4. In the public CMakeLists.txt the per-target ISA flags are PRIVATE to the Benchmark-* executables (tests/benchmark.cpp) and do not reach the qHilbert static library (source/qHilbert.cpp) that holds the SIMD paths, so a build as written runs the same generic serial code in every target; the flags actually used for the table's columns are not public. Each trial is only 16,384 points (microsecond-scale timing). Compiler not stated. 2018 numbers; repo abandoned since 2018-12-31.

workload: C++20 SIMD wrapper with a math function library for SSE2 to AVX-512, NEON/ASIMD and fixed-size SVE; the repo has a benchmarks/module harness (nanobench) but no published results.
claimed_speedup: No numbers: README says the goal is 'an efficient, low-level, high-abstraction library suited for high performance' and cites three papers (PACT 2012, HPCS 2018, a 2014-era Scalable Computing article) without summarizing results.
tradeoffs: Requires C++20; fixed-size SVE only; marked 'operational' with possible performance issues remaining.
caveats: No benchmark numbers in the README or repo; benchmarks/ has only the nanobench harness (CMakeLists.txt, experiment.hpp, generators.hpp, nanobench.h, module/ with algorithm, combinatorial, core, math and special subdirectories) and no result tables. The README calls EVE a research project first, with API and minimum compiler subject to change before a 0.1 release, and says some performance issues may remain. Documentation and the cited papers (PACT 2012 Boost.SIMD, HPCS 2018 small matrix-vector, Scalable Computing EVE article) live on github.io, ACM and HAL pages that were blocked here. Lead for a retier: Felix Rocke's April 2023 LMU bachelor thesis 'Evaluation of C++ SIMD Libraries' benchmarks six SIMD libraries against intrinsics on AVX2, AVX-512, SVE and NEON (abstract, snippet only: several libraries matched intrinsics, Highway strongest on the integer case study); whether EVE is among the six was not confirmed (nm.ifi.lmu.de blocked). Requires C++20 (g++ 13+, clang++ 16+, MSVC 19.44+); no dynamic-size SVE.

name: Pare
language: C (x264, SVT-AV1, libvmaf) compiled to WebAssembly SIMD128 with Emscripten, TypeScript web app
baseline: ffmpeg.wasm 0.12 (x264 built without its assembly) single-threaded and multithreaded; native x264 as the ceiling
workload: Compress Big Buck Bunny (10 s, 30.7 MB) to at least 50% smaller at matching VMAF NEG in headless Chrome, including the size plan and test encodes, on a 4-core 8-thread cloud VM.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md 'Speed in context' (Big Buck Bunny, 10 s, 30.7 MB): Pare 24.9 s from the click, including the size plan and Auto's test encodes (13.4 MB, VMAF NEG 93.1, worst frame 88.9), vs ffmpeg.wasm 0.12 single-threaded x264 `faster` CRF 19 158.9 s and multithreaded 42.4 s (both 12.2 MB, VMAF NEG 93.0, worst frame 89.8): 6.4x and 1.7x as fast per the page; native ffmpeg x264 with Pare's settings 6.4 s. Pare's encode alone took 12.9 s, about twice native x264 on the same cores. README/RESEARCH.md: about 1,500 lines of WebAssembly SIMD128 kernels make encoding 2.0-2.3x faster per core than the plain C build with byte-identical output, and the single-thread WebAssembly build runs at 54% of native x264 with the same settings (4.25 vs 7.85 fps on park).
compiler_and_flags: emcc -O3 -msimd128 (x264 configured with --extra-cflags=-O3; the threaded build adds -pthread), x264-wasm/build.sh; Emscripten version not pinned; browser is Playwright's Chromium build 1243 (playwright-core 1.63.0, research/benchmark.mjs); baseline ffmpeg.wasm is @ffmpeg/core and @ffmpeg/core-mt 0.12.10 with @ffmpeg/ffmpeg 0.12.15 (research/ffmpeg-wasm/package.json)
hardware: Xeon Platinum 8259CL 2.5 GHz (2019), 4 cores / 8 threads cloud VM shared with other work, no GPU
tradeoffs: GPL because of x264; needs WebAssembly SIMD128 and Web Workers; chunked parallel encoding costs 4-9% more bytes than a single encode; the app picks its own rate factor to hit a size target;
caveats: First-party and very new (94 commits, first in late September 2026, 3 stars). The headline 6.4x/1.7x over ffmpeg.wasm is a whole-pipeline comparison, not a kernel one: Pare adds chunked multi-worker encoding, WebCodecs decoding and its own x264 settings (diamond motion search and no 8x8-and-smaller inter partitions, about two thirds of the CPU time of the `faster`-based setting), while ffmpeg.wasm ran stock `faster` CRF 19; ffmpeg.wasm also produced a smaller file (12.2 MB vs 13.4 MB) at the same VMAF NEG with a better worst frame, and Pare's time includes finding its own rate factor. The cleanest kernel claim (2.0-2.3x per core over scalar C WebAssembly) is a sentence in RESEARCH.md without a per-kernel table. One run per row on a 4-core cloud VM shared with other work (the page reports up to 25 s variation between identical encodes in a busy session). Emscripten version unpinned. ffmpeg/ffmpeg is already catalogued; x264 itself was not in the known list.

name: DuckDB-Wasm
language: C++ (DuckDB) compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten, TypeScript API
baseline: Arquero (JavaScript dataframe library) and SQLite WASM; danfo also in the table
workload: Third-party in-browser benchmark on 1,000,000 Bandcamp sales rows (24 columns): analytical SELECTs (overall metrics, group by day, top 5 countries per item and slug type, random rows) plus index, update, insert and delete tests, run on a separate browser thread.
claimed_speedup: Independent repo (timlrx/browser-data-processing-benchmarks README; times in seconds, Date.now() difference / 1000 in index.js), i7-1165G7 with Chrome 116: Test 1 top-level metrics Arquero 0.067 s vs DuckDB-Wasm 0.014 s (4.8x, derived from page data); Test 2 group by day 1.05 s vs 0.163 s (6.4x, derived from page data); Test 3 top 5 countries 4.847 s vs 0.114 s (42x, derived from page data); Test 4 10 random rows 0.517 s vs 0.032 s (16x, derived from page data). Against in-memory SQLite WASM without indexes DuckDB-Wasm also wins Tests 1-4 (e.g. Test 1 0.376 s vs 0.014 s, 27x, derived from page data). On the M2 MacBook Air with Firefox 117 the Arquero gaps are smaller (Test 3 0.852 s vs 0.132 s, 6.5x; Test 2 0.634 s vs 0.169 s, 3.8x; derived from page data). DuckDB-Wasm loses the load step (4.309 s vs Arquero 2.866 s and SQLite 0.893 s on Chrome), loses to indexed SQLite on Tests 2 and 4 (0.005 s and 0.002 s vs 0.163 s and 0.032 s), and loses every transactional test to in-memory SQLite WASM (1000 indexed selects 1.048 s vs 0.054 s, 1000 inserts 1.397 s vs 0.041 s, 1000 deletes 2.376 s vs 0.035 s). VLDB 2022 paper abstract (search snippet only): outperforms previous data processing libraries for the Web on TPC-H at multiple scale factors; no figures seen.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1165G7 @2.80GHz Windows laptop with Chrome 116; Apple M2 MacBook Air with Firefox 117
tradeoffs: Large WASM download; extensions such as Parquet, JSON and ICU are autoloaded lazily; HTTP stack differs from native DuckDB (CORS and HTTPS required); weaker than SQLite WASM on small transactional updates.
caveats: The VLDB PDF (vldb.org), duckdb.org and ir.cwi.nl were not reachable (DNS-blocked here); the paper claim comes from a search snippet, though the repo's packages/benchmarks/src holds TPC-H suites for DuckDB-Wasm, sql.js, Arquero and Lovefield that match the snippet's comparison set. The independent repo (7 stars, 23 commits) is a single run per browser on one machine, timed in seconds with Date.now() around a Comlink call to a web worker (so worker messaging and 1 ms clock resolution are included in the 0.002-0.03 s rows); its README says fetch and load timings are noisy. It pins old packages (@duckdb/duckdb-wasm ^1.27.0, @sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm ^3.43.0-build3, arquero ^5.2.0, 2023), and the workloads are not identical: the Arquero group-by-day test also sorts its output, which the DuckDB query does not. DuckDB-Wasm is slower to load than Arquero and SQLite and far slower than SQLite WASM on point lookups, updates, inserts and deletes; its wins are analytical scans and aggregations. No comparison against native DuckDB (the category's 'same library compiled natively' baseline) was found. Default build is single-threaded; multithreading is experimental.

name: Loro
language: Rust compiled to WebAssembly with JavaScript bindings
baseline: Yjs 13.6.11 (pure-JS CRDT library); the same table also lists ywasm 0.9.3 and Automerge 2.1.10 (both wasm)
workload: dmonad/crdt-benchmarks suite on Node 20.5.0: B1 no conflicts, B2 two users with conflicts, B3 many conflicts, B4 replay of a real-world editing trace (259,778 operations) at N=6000.
claimed_speedup: dmonad/crdt-benchmarks README, N=6000, i5-8400, Node 20.5.0, loro 0.10.1 vs yjs 13.6.11: B4 apply real-world editing dataset 3,089 ms vs 5,714 ms (1.85x, derived from page data); B4x100 309,689 ms vs 608,908 ms (2.0x, derived from page data); B4 parseTime 13 ms vs 39 ms; B1.1 append N characters 120 ms vs 188 ms; B1.4 79 ms vs 131 ms; B1.5 82 ms vs 154 ms; B3.1 56 ms vs 75 ms. Mixed: Yjs is faster on B2.2 (65 vs 83 ms), B2.3 (85 vs 112 ms), B2.4 (178 vs 208 ms), B3.3 (86 vs 116 ms), B3.4 (72 vs 227 ms) and trivially on B1.6, B1.9 and B2.1; Loro's encodeTime is far higher (B4 77 ms vs 11 ms, B4x100 14,429 ms vs 365 ms, B2.4 233 ms vs 12 ms), its documents are larger (B4 258,228 vs 159,929 bytes) and its bundle is 15x larger (1,052,250 vs 69,124 bytes; 399,276 vs 20,100 gzipped).
tradeoffs: Bundle size 1,052,250 bytes vs Yjs 69,124 bytes; larger update messages (B1.1 average update size 109 vs 27 bytes). Compared with ywasm and Automerge (both wasm) Loro is also faster on B4 (28,675 ms and 14,326 ms).
caveats: Third-party shootout maintained by the Yjs author, so the competitor ran it; wasm compiler flags are not stated. The results table is old: crdt-benchmarks' last commit is 2024-02-12 and the table measures loro 0.10.1 (now 1.x) and ywasm 0.9.3. The harness uses Loro's snapshot export by default (exportSnapshot stores the in-memory state, which lowers parseTime but enlarges docSize and encodeTime) and batches cached remote updates with importUpdateBatch inside a transaction. memUsed excludes wasm runtime memory, so Loro's 0 B rows are not comparable with Yjs's JS heap figures. Gains are workload-specific: Yjs wins most concurrent-conflict text/array workloads (B2.2-B2.4, B3.3, B3.4), all encode times and bundle size.

hardware: 2015 MacBook Pro (CPU model not given)
name: absurd-sql
language: JavaScript backend for SQLite compiled to WebAssembly (sql.js)
baseline: IndexedDB used directly in the browser
workload: SQLite on top of IndexedDB blocks: read 'SELECT SUM(value) FROM kv' and bulk insert, compared with plain IndexedDB, in Chrome.
claimed_speedup: README: 'It consistently beats IndexedDB performance up to 10x' for reads and bulk-insert writes (shown only as chart images, no numbers readable).
tradeoffs: Needs SharedArrayBuffer (cross-origin isolation headers); Safari fallback allows only one writing tab at a time; relies on sql.js (SQLite WASM).
caveats: First-party only; the headline 'up to 10x' is the only number in text, and the chart images (user-images.githubusercontent.com) could not be opened here, so per-test values were not read. Hardware is a 2015 MacBook Pro with no CPU model; Chrome version not stated. Baseline harness (src/examples/bench/queries-raw-idb.js) is the slowest raw-IndexedDB pattern: sumAll walks an openCursor one record per step and populate issues one store.put per row, while absurd-sql packs rows into 4096-byte SQLite blocks; Nolan Lawson's follow-up post 'Speeding up IndexedDB reads and writes' (2021-08-22) argued batched getAll()/getAllKeys() pagination and relaxed durability close much of that gap (search snippet only: in Chrome a 50,000-row cursor read took 1194.2 vs 488.3 with 1,000-item batches, units not shown). Timing is asymmetric: the SQLite sumAll timer starts after db.prepare, the raw-IDB timer includes opening the transaction. The harness's populateLarge inserts 400,000 rows. Requires the author's sql.js fork (@jlongster/sql.js), SharedArrayBuffer with COOP/COEP headers, and a worker; Hackaday's write-up (snippet only) says native SQLite is 2-3x faster than absurd-sql. This is a storage-layer win over the IndexedDB API, not a wasm compute win. Last commit 2023-08-06 (a merged @actualbudget patch); abandoned.

name: BenchmarkingWebAssembly (Understanding the Performance of WebAssembly Applications)
language: C (PolyBenchC and CHStone) compiled by Cheerp to WebAssembly and JavaScript; Python test scripts
baseline: JavaScript produced from the same C programs by Cheerp 2.0
workload: 41 PolyBenchC and CHStone benchmarks plus other subjects at extra-small, small and medium input sizes, WASM vs JS execution time in Chrome 79, Firefox 71 and Edge 79, desktop and mobile.
claimed_speedup: README RQ1: with extra-small and small inputs WebAssembly is faster than JavaScript in almost all benchmarks (97.6% and 95.1%), averaging 26.99x (extra-small) and 8.22x (small); with medium inputs 18 of 41 benchmarks become slower in WebAssembly (average slowdown 1.71x) and the remaining 23 average 6.70x faster. Example: 3mm is 47.71x, 10.54x and 1.12x faster in WebAssembly for extra-small, small and medium inputs. WebAssembly also uses 3.39-6.20x more memory than JavaScript across browsers.
compiler_and_flags: Cheerp 2.0, tested at -O1, -O2, -Ofast and -Oz (README); Chrome 79, Firefox 71, Edge 79
tradeoffs: A study, not a library: the JS baseline is machine-generated by Cheerp rather than idiomatic hand-written JavaScript, and WASM's advantage shrinks or reverses as input grows; repo has no license, so the code is reference only.
caveats: A measurement study (IMC 2021 artifact) rather than a reusable library: the 'project' is Cheerp 2.0's WebAssembly output, and the JavaScript baseline is Cheerp's own JS output from the same C sources, not hand-written JS. Mixed outcome: the WebAssembly lead shrinks with input size and reverses for 18 of 41 benchmarks at medium inputs; WebAssembly uses 3.4-6.2x more memory. Browsers are from 2019-2020 (Chrome 79, Firefox 71, Edge 79), hardware is not stated in the README, and timings are copied manually from the browser console. language: C++ compiled to WebAssembly and to an N-API addon, JavaScript harness

claimed_speedup: Fibonacci: WebAssembly 11,508,910 ops/s vs N-API addon 5,204,691 and JS 4,044,156. Fermat primality: WebAssembly 2,402,964 vs addon 1,833,692 and JS 1,678,845. SHA256: addon 67,807, WebAssembly 34,445, JS 13,453. WebAssembly loses on Levenshtein (210,776 vs addon 308,924 and JS 295,433) and on simple linear regression (WebAssembly 37,117 and 42,521 with TypedArrays vs JS 291,985).
compiler_and_flags: WASM: emcc --bind -std=c++14 src/wasm.cpp -s WASM=1 -s SINGLE_FILE=1 -O3 (package.json build:wasm; Emscripten version not stated). Addon: node-gyp rebuild --release with default node-gyp Release flags (binding.gyp sets no extra flags). Node version not stated.
tradeoffs: Mixed result by design: WASM beats the same C++ built as an addon when per-call overhead dominates (Fibonacci, Fermat) but loses where data is copied across the boundary (regression, Levenshtein).

WebAssembly is fastest on only 2 of 5 tasks (Fibonacci, Fermat); it beats pure JS on 3 of 5 (also SHA256, 34,445 vs 13,453 ops/s, about 2.6x derived from page data) but loses to JS on Levenshtein and linear regression and to the N-API addon on Levenshtein, regression and SHA256. The Fibonacci kernel is tail-recursive, which the C++ compiler turns into a loop while JS has no tail calls, so that row mostly measures tail-call elimination. benchmark.js draws random inputs on every call and its randomInRange helper ignores its min argument (Fibonacci n ranges 0-45, not 30-45); inputs are identically distributed for all three implementations. name: wasmoon
language: C (official Lua 5.4) compiled to WebAssembly, TypeScript bindings
baseline: Fengari (Lua VM rewritten in JavaScript)

name: xxhash-wasm
language: WebAssembly with JavaScript wrapper (implementation of xxHash 32-bit and 64-bit)
baseline: xxhashjs (pure JavaScript xxHash, uses cuint for 64-bit math); also Node built-in crypto md5 and sha1 (different, cryptographic algorithms)
workload: XXH64/XXH32 hashing via the public JS API. Third-party: byte-array one-shot (4 B, 8 B), 1 MiB bulk, streaming 1 MiB in 64 B-64 KiB chunks, and ASCII strings (8, 32 chars). First-party README: Benchmark.js ops/sec on random ASCII strings from 1 byte to 100,000,000 bytes, plus Node crypto md5/sha1 for comparison.
claimed_speedup: Third-party (haya32x64 docs/benchmarks.md, snapshot 2026-08-09, xxhash-wasm 1.1.0 vs xxhashjs 0.2.2, public API, medians of nine 150 ms samples): XXH64 one-shot 4-byte input 39.4 ns vs 1939.3 ns on C8a (AMD EPYC 9R45), about 49x (derived from page data), and 63.9 vs 2691.0 ns on C8g (Neoverse V2), about 42x (derived). 1 MiB bulk 15,973 vs 37 MB/s (about 432x, derived) on C8a and 10,738 vs 28 MB/s (about 384x, derived) on C8g. 8-char strings 59.2 vs 2437.8 ns (about 41x, derived). First-party README (Benchmark.js ops/sec): the prose says the 32-bit hash is up to 90x and the 64-bit up to 350x faster than xxhashjs. The table itself shows 32-bit from 11.2x at 1 byte (5,752,446 vs 513,517 ops/sec) up to 140.7x at 1,000,000 bytes, and 64-bit from 373x at 1 byte (4,438,501 vs 11,896 ops/sec) up to 677.8x at 100,000 bytes. At 100,000,000 bytes 64-bit is 34.56 vs 0.13 ops/sec (265.8x). All README ratios are derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Hand-written src/xxhash.wat built with wasm-opt --enable-bulk-memory -O4 (package.json build-wasm script; npm 1.1.0 artifact). Third-party run under Node.js 24.18.0 / V8 13.6.233.17-node.50 via node --expose-gc js.mjs (haya32x64 bench/, calibration plus warmup, then nine 150 ms samples, median). The first-party README table comes from bench/index.js (Benchmark.js, node --max-old-space-size=4096 index.js), with Node 17.3 stated for the Node-crypto table.
hardware: Third-party: AWS EC2 c8a.2xlarge (AMD EPYC 9R45) and c8g.2xlarge (Arm Neoverse V2), Ubuntu 26.04, timed work pinned to CPU 2. First-party README: an x64 MacBook Pro (CPU model not stated) running Node 17.3; the xxhash-wasm 64-bit column is identical in the xxhashjs and Node-crypto tables, so both appear to come from the same run (inference).
tradeoffs: Needs BigInt in WASM, bulk memory and TextEncoder.encodeInto (Chrome >= 85, Firefox >= 79, Safari >= 15, Node >= 15); older xxhash-wasm 0.4.2 is 3-4x slower. WASM instantiation takes about 1 ms in the browser and a little over 2 ms in Node. Small bundle (11.4 kB minified, 2.3 kB gzipped) versus xxhashjs 41.5 kB.
caveats: The baseline xxhashjs is a slow pure-JS port that emulates 64-bit math with cuint, not a tuned JS hash. The Node crypto comparison uses cryptographic md5/sha1. There is no native xxHash C baseline. The README prose (up to 90x/350x) understates its own table (up to ~141x/~678x, derived). In the first-party bench/index.js the xxhashjs calls also run .toString(16) on each result while xxhash-wasm returns raw numbers/BigInt, so the baseline does extra work (small at large inputs). Not the fastest wasm xxHash: hash-wasm 4.10.0's README shows XXHash64 at 101.66 MB/s vs xxhash-wasm 1.0.2's 47.58 MB/s at 32 bytes (2.1x, derived), with a tie at 1 MB (15,989 vs 15,929 MB/s). In haya32x64's harness, pure-JS haya32x64 (a different hash) beats xxhash-wasm XXH64 on 4-byte keys (22.9 vs 39.4 ns), and cyrb53 (53-bit) is faster still. The third-party measurer is a competing hash author's new repo (a wave-7 catalog entry), with one instance per host type. WebAssembly instantiation (~1-2 ms) is excluded. Needs BigInt-in-wasm, bulk memory and TextEncoder.encodeInto (Chrome 85+, Safari 15+, Node 15+).

workload: Go benchmarks over tiny hand-written .wat modules: Fib(20) recursive, 100k-iteration Sum loop, 64KiB MemRW, module Instantiate (decode+validate+instantiate), plus JIT-mode kernels Sort (10k i32 quicksort), Dispatch (br_table), Hash, Mandel, Indirect (call_indirect).
claimed_speedup: Interpreter vs wazero interpreter (Apple M3, ns/op): Fib 974,787 vs 1,787,663; Sum 3,014,618 vs 3,930,498; MemRW 4,751,546 vs 5,153,545; Instantiate 2,129 vs 14,100; README says 1.1-1.8x faster than wazero's interpreter, 1.5-2.4x faster than wagon, about 2x faster than life, instantiation 3-14x faster. JIT vs wazero compiler: MemRW 39,575 vs 70,643, Sort 367,952 vs 477,368, Sum 27,112 vs 26,850 (level), Fib 41,187 vs 37,832 (slower), Indirect 3,926,713 vs 2,812,512 (1.4x slower); on dual EPYC 7K62 Sum 2.0x and MemRW 1.6x ahead of wazero compiler, Fib 1.6x behind.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.24 (per bench/README.md); go test -bench . -benchmem ./bench with default Go flags; fixtures compiled from .wat with wat2wasm and checked in. bench/go.mod at HEAD declares go 1.25.0 and pins wazero v1.12.0, wagon v0.4.0 (via replace) and life at a 2019 commit. Every timed iteration checks the returned value against a constant.
hardware: Apple M3 (main tables); dual AMD EPYC 7K62 server for the amd64 JIT comparison
tradeoffs: Pure Go with zero dependencies (no cgo), interpreter by default; optional tiered JIT (EnableJIT) only on arm64 and amd64 and per-function interpreter fallback (optimizing tier covers about 86% of spec-suite function bodies). The README claims full official spec-suite conformance, metering and interruption support.
caveats: Self-benchmarked by the author. Each row is a single run with no variance reported, and run-to-run noise is visible: the wasman interpreter's Fib reads 974,787 ns in the main table and 1,120,975 ns in the JIT table, 15% apart, which is larger than the 1.08x MemRW margin over wazero's interpreter. Workloads are very small (Fib(20) is about 13.5k calls). The Instantiate sub-benchmark for wazero creates and closes a whole wazero Runtime on every iteration (NewRuntimeWithConfig + Instantiate + Close, with no CompiledModule reuse), so the 6.6x instantiation win over wazero includes runtime setup and teardown that wasman's row does not pay. The README bolds wasman-jit on Sum even though its 27,112 ns is 1% slower than wazero-compiler's 26,850 ns. The EPYC 7K62 claims (Sum 2.0x, MemRW 1.6x ahead, Fib 1.6x behind) are ratios only, with no table. Only Go engines are compared: cgo runtimes (wasmtime-go, wasmer-go) are excluded, so there is no comparison with wasmtime, wasmer, V8 or WAMR. The JIT result is mixed: ahead of wazero's compiler on memory-bound code (MemRW 1.8x, Sort 1.3x), level on Sum and Dispatch, and behind on Fib (9%), Hash (9%), Mandel (3%) and Indirect (1.4x). LICENSE carries 'Copyright (c) 2020 @mathetake', the author of gasm, which became wazero, so wasman shares ancestry with its main baseline. Interpreter and JIT correctness fixes landed 2026-08-16 to 08-19, after the documented numbers (host-call resolution, toll return sentinel). None of them touches the benchmark workloads, which have no imports and no TollStation. Wazero is the Go incumbent but not one of the listed baselines.

name: Cage (wasmtime-mte, MTE-based memory safety and bounds checking for 64-bit Wasm)
baseline: Plain 64-bit Wasm (wasm64/memory64) run in Wasmtime without MTE, where the sandbox relies on software bounds checks; the paper reports speedups 'over wasm64' (search snippet of arXiv 2408.11456; whether the baseline build is upstream Wasmtime or the fork with MTE off was not confirmed).
workload: PolyBench/C kernels compiled to 64-bit Wasm with Cage's LLVM fork and run in the wasmtime-mte fork on a Google Pixel 8 (per search snippets of the paper); Cage offloads the wasm64 sandbox bounds check to Arm MTE and adds MTE heap/stack safety and PAC pointer protection.
claimed_speedup: cage-meta README abstract: memory-safety runtime overhead <5.8% and memory overhead <5.3% (the BibTeX abstract on the same page says <3.7%), and MTE-based sandboxing 'achieving a speedup of over 5.1%'. Search snippet of arXiv 2408.11456 (snippet only): on a Google Pixel 8 (Tensor G3), PolyBench/C mean speedup of MTE sandboxing over wasm64 of 3.7±6.5%, 5.1±4.0% and 33.9±2.4% on the three core types (33.9% on the in-order Cortex-A510 cores); memory safety plus MTE sandboxing 2.1±5.6%, 4.5±4.1% and 29.2±2.5% versus wasm64.
compiler_and_flags: LLVM fork (TUM-DSE/llvm-memsafe-wasm) and wasi-libc fork; flags not stated on the pages opened
hardware: Google Pixel 8 (Google Tensor G3) with Arm MTE and PAC, per the paper's artifact appendix as quoted in a search snippet; LLVM, wasmtime and benchmarks cross-compiled on an x86 host. Not confirmed from an opened page.
tradeoffs: Needs Arm CPUs with MTE and PAC, 64-bit Wasm (memory64) modules, and the authors' forks of LLVM, wasmtime, wasm-tools and wasi-libc; the wasmtime fork carries the upstream Apache-2.0 LICENSE file but cage-meta has no LICENSE file. Primary purpose is memory safety; the speedup is a side effect of replacing software bounds checks.
caveats: The CGO 2025 paper (doi 10.1145/3696443.3708920, pp. 538-552), arXiv 2408.11456, the CGO slides on dse.in.tum.de and the Zenodo artifact (doi 10.5281/zenodo.13772996) were all unreachable here; per-core numbers come from search snippets only. The 5.1% is a mean with a ±4.0% spread on one core type; on the big cores the mean is 3.7% with a ±6.5% spread (spread larger than the mean), and only the in-order Cortex-A510 shows a large gain (33.9%). The win is against wasm64 software bounds checks, not against 32-bit Wasm with guard pages, which needs no explicit checks. Requires Arm MTE hardware (Pixel 8 class). README abstract (memory overhead <5.3%) and BibTeX abstract (<3.7%) disagree. wasmtime-mte is a research fork of bytecodealliance/wasmtime (12,557 commits, mostly upstream; last MTE commits 2026-01-14), not upstreamed; its README is the stock wasmtime README with no MTE instructions.

name: VectorVisor (GPU binary translator for WebAssembly)
baseline: Same Wasm modules on CPU with Wasmtime embedded in VectorVisor (--wasmtime=true) and native x86-64 Rust builds (cargo run --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu), on 4-vCPU AWS c5.xlarge (Intel) or c5a.xlarge (AMD) instances; hand-written CUDA versions (cuda-blockhash, cuda-blur) on the GPU for imagehash and imageblur.
workload: Serverless-style benchmarks (scrypt, pbkdf2, imageblur, imagehash, genpdf, lz4 compression, nlp, average) run as thousands of concurrent Wasm instances on a GPU versus CPU instances.
claimed_speedup: USENIX ATC 2023 abstract (search snippet only; usenix.org and the Princeton PDF were unreachable): throughput-per-dollar up to 2.9x compared with Intel x86-64 VMs in the cloud, for certain classes of compute-bound workloads, and in some cases matching the throughput-per-dollar of native CUDA baselines. No numbers on the repo pages opened; readme.md says the approach is 'less efficient than manual translation'.
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release; benchmark Wasm built in optimized and interleaved variants (scrypt-opt-*.wasm)
hardware: GPU side: AWS g4dn.xlarge (1 NVIDIA T4, 4 vCPU), g5.xlarge (1 NVIDIA A10G, 4 vCPU) or g4ad.xlarge (AMD Radeon Pro V520); CPU baseline: AWS c5.xlarge (Intel) or c5a.xlarge (AMD); load generator c5a.8xlarge, all in us-east-1b (benchmarks/run_benchmarks_aws.py). Exact CPU models not named on the pages opened.
tradeoffs: Needs an OpenCL 1.2+ GPU; best on NVIDIA under Linux, AMD ROCm sometimes crashes and Intel fails beyond smoke tests; workloads must be throughput-oriented (many independent requests), single-threaded Wasm, with fixed heap and stack sizes; latency per request is higher than on CPU.
caveats: Headline metric is throughput per dollar of a GPU instance versus a 4-vCPU CPU instance, not raw throughput or latency, and the 2.9x applies only to some compute-bound workloads (search snippet of the abstract; paper at https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc23/presentation/ginzburg not reachable here). The repo holds figures (latency_throughput.png, latency_breakdown.png), make_figures.py and raw result directories (2022-12-22-20:09:12 is the paper's data per benchmarks/README.md) but no text summary of results. The Wasmtime CPU baseline is VectorVisor's embedded --wasmtime mode with a pinned wasmtime version, not the standalone CLI. readme.md admits it is less efficient than manual GPU translation; AMD V520 support is partial and sometimes crashes. benchmarks/README.md says the end-to-end evaluation takes about 24 hours on AWS. Last commit 2024-09-26 (stale).

name: KinoWASM (KinoRuntime)
baseline: WAMR iwasm fast interpreter (also compared against wasm3)
workload: CoreMark 1.0 compiled to a WASI wasm module (Clang 11.0.0, -O3) and a recursive fibonacci(40) module, each run through the runtime's own CLI; interpreter versus interpreter.
claimed_speedup: CoreMark Iterations/Sec: KinoRuntime 4385.746651, wasm3 3555.555556, iwasm (WAMR fast interpreter) 1734.417344; page states approximately 1.23x wasm3 and 2.53x iwasm. fibonacci(40): KinoRuntime 1838.94 ms, wasm3 2601.12 ms, iwasm 4298.94 ms; page states approximately 1.41x wasm3 and 2.34x iwasm.
compiler_and_flags: Guest CoreMark module: Clang 11.0.0 (LLVM 176249bd6732), -O3. The fibtest.wasm guest is built locally with Emscripten emcc (WASMData/README.md; binary not in Git). Runtime executables: KinoRuntime 'standard Clang build' with compiler version and preset not recorded; wasm3 and iwasm build configurations not recorded. CMakePresets.json also offers MSVC PGO presets (x64-Release-pgo-gen/use) trained on CoreMark, described as lifting CoreMark by about 6.7%; which preset built the measured binary is unrecorded. The public build needs MSVC 14.50+ or clang-cl (guaranteed tail calls via musttail) with AVX2 enabled.
hardware: Intel Core i7-13700F, Windows 11 (user-reported)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks, 6 commits; the README says it is used in several production console titles (console integrations are private, so this cannot be checked)
tradeoffs: Interpreter (register-TOS, direct-threaded, tail calls), so far slower than JIT/AOT engines such as wasmtime or wasmer. Public repo builds only for Windows x64 and needs a compiler with guaranteed tail calls. No SIMD execution, no threads/atomics, no GC; WASI only partial; memory64 and exception handling partial. Host-controlled suspend/resume of guest execution is a feature. Embedding needs a host-provided linear-memory backend.
caveats: benchmark.md calls the numbers 'user-supplied measurements' and a 'preliminary snapshot'. There is one machine (Windows 11), and the runtime versions, runtime compiler flags, KinoRuntime preset/PGO settings, measurement date, workload hashes and per-run spread are all unrecorded. CoreMark is not bundled, and iwasm ran 30,000 iterations while the other two ran 60,000. The final CRC differs between iwasm (0x5275) and wasm3/KinoRuntime (0xbd59). That is consistent with the different iteration counts, since CoreMark's final CRC accumulates over iterations, and all three logs report validation passed. Fibonacci timing uses the in-guest clock through each runtime's WASI clock, and the repeat count is unrecorded. The baselines were Windows builds of unknown configuration. WAMR's core/config.h enables labels-as-values (computed-goto) dispatch only under __GNUC__, so an MSVC or clang-cl build of iwasm falls back to switch dispatch, which may explain much of the 2.5x gap to iwasm. wasm3 on Windows may be similarly disadvantaged. The repo carries CoreMark-trained PGO presets, which is a tuning risk if one built the measured binary. The project is very new (first commit 2026-09-30, 6 commits, single author), and correctness fixes landed 2026-10-08/09 (live register tracking below wide-arithmetic operands; integer overflow in buffer-read bounds checks), possibly after the undated measurements.

name: WasmKit register-based interpreter (swiftwasm/WasmKit)
baseline: WasmKit's own previous (second-generation) stack-based interpreter; also charted against wasm3, stitch and wasmi
workload: CoreMark compiled to Wasm, interpreted by the old and new WasmKit interpreters and, in a second chart, by wasm3, stitch and wasmi.
claimed_speedup: CoreMark score 7.4x higher than the second generation interpreter; versus wasm3, stitch and wasmi the doc only says the result is 'well competitive' (chart images only, no numbers in the text).
compiler_and_flags: WasmKit built with swift build -c release, toolchain swift-DEVELOPMENT-SNAPSHOT-2024-09-17-a; CoreMark built with wasi-sdk clang 18.1.2 -O3 -D_WASI_EMULATED_PROCESS_CLOCKS (from the CoreMark log on the same page and Benchmarks/bench.py PORT_CFLAGS)
hardware: 2020 Mac mini (M1, 16GB RAM)
license: MIT (runtime modules); the GDBRemoteProtocol and WasmKitGDBHandler modules are Apache-2.0 with a Runtime Library Exception
tradeoffs: Swift runtime; runtime modules are MIT, the GDBRemoteProtocol and WasmKitGDBHandler modules are Apache-2.0 with Runtime Library Exception. Interpreter only, no JIT or AOT; no Fixed-width SIMD claim checked.
caveats: The headline 7.4x is against WasmKit's own older stack-based interpreter, not an external incumbent. Against wasm3, stitch and wasmi the doc only shows a chart (SVG with outlined glyphs, values not readable) and says 'well competitive', so no faster-than-incumbent claim exists. The second-generation CoreMark log on the same page shows WasmKit gen-2 at 291 iterations/s, wasmi at 1321 and wasmtime (JIT) at 11527; 7.4x of 291 is about 2155 iterations/s (derived from page data), still roughly 5x below wasmtime, and the log's machine and wasmi version are not stated, so a wasmi comparison cannot be derived. The doc says 'we have not done a comprehensive performance evaluation yet'. Single machine (2020 Mac mini M1), single CoreMark run, 2024-09 toolchain snapshot, so numbers are old for the 2026 code. A Benchmarks/bench.py harness (CoreMark, wasmi-benchmarks replay, wasm3/wasmi/wasmtime engines) exists in the repo but no results report.
